watch_next: Stormwater and school committee presentations on October 20, and handbook chapters 1-6 returning at the next meeting.
The town manager's walkthrough of the school cafeteria with the superintendent, and the accessibility study the polling place vote depends on.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to designate the middle school cafeteria as the polling place, contingent on an accessibility study.
The board ratified the employment agreement for the fire chief, running from the current chief's retirement to mid-2029; the vote was unanimous.
The board accepted the findings in an open meeting law response letter and authorized the chair to sign and submit it, unanimously.
The board ratified a full-time police officer appointment, approved an earth removal renewal, and granted a class 2 auto dealer license, all unanimously.
The board adopted a revised appointment policy as amended, then discussed the special town meeting warrant without settling its articles.

why_it_matters: The polling place decision sets where residents vote, though registrars asked that the general election be held at TC Pacios rather than a school and the designation depends on an accessibility study.

Items discussed for the special town meeting warrant, including school-side funding requests and a possible transfer of free cash to a special education reserve, are ones residents may be asked to vote on, with amounts not yet set.

ours.headline: Board designated the middle-high school cafeteria as polling place and ratified a new fire chief and police officer.

watch_next: November 17 special town meeting: zoning and stormwater fee articles, plus the Brooks House sale/lease report
FY26 budget close-out figures, expected in roughly two to three weeks

what_happened.line: Select Board authorized a license agreement and waived building-department fees to advance the Food Pantry's move to 30 School Street.
A resident disputed the building commissioner's call that the new structure counts as permanent rather than temporary.
Board publicly introduced incoming town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller.
Zoning cleanup and a stormwater fee-bylaw article were referred to the planning board for the November 17 special town meeting.
Board declined to pursue a MassWorks grant this cycle to study senior housing at the former TCP school, citing a need for more public discussion.

why_it_matters: The food pantry's site status and its permanent-vs-temporary classification affect what oversight and process apply to future town-building decisions.
The stormwater bylaw change would tie fee amounts to a planning-board schedule that can change without a town meeting vote, which residents will be asked to weigh in November.
Passing on the MassWorks grant this cycle means no funded study of TCP senior housing for now, leaving that option undecided.

ours.headline: Select Board advanced the Food Pantry's temporary move to 30 School Street, waiving fees and OK'ing a license.

watch_next: Thursday's special town meeting vote on Article 1 (school aid appropriation) and Article 3 (sports restoration)

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to recommend a lower, net education-aid figure than the school committee requested for Thursday's special town meeting article.
The board voted to create a special revenue fund from Winter Recovery Assistance Program money to fund a citizen petition restoring cut middle school and some high school sports.
The board voted, unanimously and as amended, to send a letter to state legislative leaders supporting the voter-approved audit of the Massachusetts legislature.
The board approved a permit for the Eagle House supporters' fall fundraiser toll booth in town center.

why_it_matters: Thursday's special town meeting will ask voters to act on both the school aid article and the sports-restoration article the board discussed tonight, and the board's recommended aid figure differs from what the school committee asked for.
The sports article's funding source is one-time snow-and-ice relief money rather than a new line in the operating budget, which shapes what happens after this year if the article passes.
A resident's public comment tied a recent increase in state aid to whether the school budget should be treated as level-service, a question the board's article recommendation touches directly.

ours.headline: Select Board recommends a lower education-aid figure than the school committee for Thursday's special town meeting article.

watch_next: Select Board meeting September 1, 2026 -- expected decision on WRAP funds and town meeting article recommendations
Special town meeting warrant closes September 17, 2026, ahead of the November 17 town meeting

what_happened.line: The Select Board ratified Jessica Jack Miller as assistant town manager, effective September 8.
The board held off deciding how to apply new state winter-storm relief funds against the FY26 snow-and-ice deficit, pending word from the School and Finance Committees.
The board granted the food pantry permission to use temporary trailers at 30 School Street once a use agreement is drafted.
The board set warrant open and close dates for a special town meeting on November 17, 2026.
The board declared a 1998 ambulance surplus and closed a utility pole petition hearing.

why_it_matters: The snow-and-ice deficit decision affects how a budget shortfall gets closed -- by a transfer, a reappropriation of state funds, or some mix -- with the amount still unconfirmed pending a state review.
The food pantry's move to temporary trailers affects a service residents rely on after its current site loses heat this winter.
The November special town meeting warrant will carry articles residents will be asked to vote on, including any snow-and-ice or state-aid items now under discussion.

ours.headline: Select Board ratified Jessica Jack Miller as assistant town manager, deferred snow-and-ice relief funds decision

what_happened.line: Select Board members, the facilities director, and the town's building design committee toured Brooks House and the former TCP school in person to assess condition.
A food pantry representative questioned whether Brooks House can hold the pantry, citing water, bathroom, and floor-load needs, with no alternative site ready by October 1st.
The tour covered TCP's boiler leaks, asbestos-related ceiling costs, and ADA-trigger cost thresholds on roof work, with several cost figures described as estimates still to be confirmed.
A board member asked what basis existed for a roof-cost figure presented at a 2023 special town meeting; the facilities director said no formal roofer estimate existed at that time.
No votes were taken on the properties; the meeting ended with a vote to adjourn.

why_it_matters: Any eventual decision on Brooks House or TCP — including where the food pantry operates — will carry repair, ADA-compliance, and asbestos-abatement costs that a future town meeting may be asked to fund.
Whether roof or renovation work crosses an ADA-trigger cost threshold changes the scope and cost of any project at TCP, which affects what gets proposed to voters.
The pantry's relocation options remain unresolved, which matters to anyone who relies on that service or lives near either building.

ours.headline: Select Board and design committee toured Brooks House and TCP in person to assess building condition ahead of a future decision on the properties.

watch_next: September 1 Select Board meeting, where warrant petitioners may present their articles
September 3 special town meeting vote on the three warrant articles

what_happened.line: The Select Board approved the September 3 special town meeting warrant, including three articles on the FY27 school budget shortfall and restoring middle school athletics and transportation.
The board voted unanimously to add the school committee's own shortfall article to that warrant.

The town manager said no certified free cash exists yet for the citizen petition seeking a free cash transfer, and town counsel is still reviewing which fund types the article's available funds language can legally draw from.
The next Select Board meeting is set for September 1, likely including warrant petitioners presenting their articles ahead of the September 3 vote.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at the September 3 special town meeting to vote on additional money for the FY27 school operating budget and on restoring middle school sports and student-athlete transportation.
One of the three articles names a funding source, certified free cash or available funds, that town officials say is not yet certified and may not be confirmed as usable before the vote.
Two of the three articles address the same school shortfall and were left unresolved as written, so town meeting itself may need to sort out overlap between them.

ours.headline: The Select Board placed the school district's shortfall articles on the September special town meeting warrant.

watch_next: Building tour of TC Pacios and Brooks House, August 11 at 4:00 p.m.
Finalized September 3rd special town meeting warrant, expected at the August 10th select board meeting

what_happened.line: The board told the facilities director to prepare separated cost estimates for repairing versus demolishing the failing TC Pacios building before any town meeting article.
Both bids for the 100 Laura Lane sewer connection were rejected, one for missing paperwork and one for exceeding budget; the town will do part of the work in-house.
The board ratified a new principal assessor and part-time principal clerk and appointed a new Green Communities associate member.
A tour of TC Pacios and Brooks House with the Municipal Building Design Committee was scheduled for August 11th.
The town manager said a rumored citizens petition to spend FY26 free cash on athletics cannot go to the September 3rd special town meeting because that free cash will not be certified by DLS in time.

why_it_matters: The direction on TC Pacios starts the process toward a future town meeting vote on repairing or tearing down the building, which will carry a capital cost either way.
The rejected sewer bids mean the 100 Laura Lane connection will take a mixed in-house/vendor approach, which can affect its cost and schedule.
Residents watching the September 3rd special town meeting warrant should note that a free-cash-funded athletics article, if brought forward, cannot legally be voted on that date.

ours.headline: Board directed staff to develop repair-vs-demolition cost estimates for the failing TC Pacios building.

watch_next: Formal committee recommendation and vote on TC Pacios and Brooks House at a future meeting
Building Design Committee meeting, August 3rd

what_happened.line: Select Board and the building design committee leaned toward demolishing TC Pacios rather than repairing it, with no formal vote taken.
The Facilities Director was tasked with cost estimates for either a roof replacement or asbestos abatement plus full demolition, to feed the FY28 capital plan.
A roof-repair fund had been double-appropriated after a 2023 transfer was never reflected in MUNIS; town meeting corrected it this past May.
Election voting equipment and polling are being permanently moved out of TC Pacios to the schools, with a mobile trailer for storage.
The committee was asked to bring formal recommendations on both TC Pacios and Brooks House to a future meeting; its next meeting is August 3rd.

why_it_matters: Whether TC Pacios is repaired or demolished will shape the FY28 capital plan and what residents are asked to fund next.
The building's boiler failed a required state inspection and needs repair within 30 days or the town faces state fines, a cost pressure independent of the long-term decision.
Moving the polling location and election storage out of TC Pacios changes where some residents vote.

ours.headline: Select Board leaned toward demolishing TC Pacios rather than repairing it, pending a formal committee vote.

watch_next: The September 3, 2026 special town meeting and its outcome on the citizen-petition warrant article
Confirmation of a temporary or deputy moderator (Rob Bowen) able to serve that night

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to call a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, 2026, opening the warrant July 28 and closing it August 7.
The board is still working to line up a stand-in moderator for that night, since town moderator Tim Murphy told the board he is unavailable September 3.
The board approved the warrant for the September 1 state primary election.
The board ratified the DPW collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local 170, following an earlier executive-session vote.
The board chose to keep running the special town meeting's legal ad in the weekly Ledger rather than switch to the daily Sentinel.

why_it_matters: The September 3 special town meeting is where residents act on the citizen petition's warrant article, and the schedule set here fixes the deadlines for that vote.
Who presides as moderator affects how that meeting is run, and the board is still confirming a deputy or temporary moderator can serve.
The ratified DPW union contract sets pay and working terms that flow into future town budgets.

ours.headline: The Select Board called a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, setting the warrant and hearing schedule.

watch_next: Select board meeting Monday, July 27, to set the special town meeting date
Finance Committee hearing on the state-aid warrant article

what_happened.line: The select board heard the school committee's request for a warrant article adding state aid to the FY27 school budget but took no vote on it.
A citizens' petition has forced an earlier special town meeting than the board had planned.
The board's own figure for the net increase in education aid, after assessments, is still pending Finance Committee review.
The board approved the 2026 special town election warrant unanimously.
The board approved an Eagle Scout loafing shed project at the DPW yard and appointed Richard Howard to the Trust Fund Commission.

why_it_matters: Residents will eventually be asked to vote at a special town meeting on an article appropriating additional state aid to the school operating budget, though the select board has not yet voted on placing it and the exact amount is still being worked out.

The spending plan behind that request changed between the school committee's July 8 and July 15 meetings, and any warrant article involving money still requires a Finance Committee hearing before it goes to voters.
The petition changes the town meeting's timing, so the date itself — set to be discussed at a board meeting the following Monday — is something residents should track.

ours.headline: A citizens' petition forced an earlier special town meeting to consider added state aid for the school budget.

watch_next: A joint meeting between the Select Board and the Municipal Building Design Committee on TCP, planned for mid-to-late August 2026
The Select Board's report on Brooks House sale or lease options, targeted for the fall town meeting

what_happened.line: The board set a path toward deciding whether to demolish or renovate the deteriorating TCP building, asking the Municipal Building Design Committee for a formal recommendation to feed fall capital planning.
The board directed staff to draft its overdue, town-meeting-directed report on selling or long-term leasing the Brooks House, targeted for completion by the fall town meeting.

The Finance Committee and Select Board approved FY2026 year-end transfers, covering legal expenses, the sealer of weights and measures, and town report printing, drawn from a vacant planning board salary line.
The board voted to approve the Town Manager's proposed FY27 goals, including a review of outsourcing payroll processing and work toward adopting several tabled financial policies.

why_it_matters: Whichever way the TCP decision goes, the cost was described as able to consume most or all of a year's capital plan, which shapes what other town projects can be funded that year.
The Brooks House report determines the town's public path for a building it has been directed by town meeting to resolve, and residents may see options at a future town meeting.
Financial policies under discussion -- OPEB funding, reserves, and revenue projections -- bear on the town's long-term borrowing capacity and, eventually, the tax rate.

ours.headline: Select Board moves toward a decision on demolishing or renovating the deteriorating TCP building

watch_next: Special town election warrant, expected back on the agenda the following week
Trust Fund Commission appointment of Richard Howard, targeted for the July 20 agenda

what_happened.line: The board tabled ratification of the new DPW union contract after labor counsel flagged discrepancies to resolve.
The board voted to take a temporary easement at 890 Flatill Road by eminent domain to keep the bridge project moving.
A dispute over how the town processed Richard Howard's Trust Fund Commission application went unresolved, with the appointment pushed to a future agenda.
Approval of the August 8 special town election warrant was put off a week so town counsel can review new mailing-notice language.
The board also adopted the current IRS mileage rate, named a new detective and other appointees, and reviewed executive-session employment agreements for several town staff.

why_it_matters: A stalled union contract leaves DPW workers' pay and terms unresolved and keeps a labor cost decision open for the town.
The eminent domain action affects a specific property owner on Flatill Road and clears the way for a town bridge project residents depend on.
The election warrant delay and the mailing-notice review could affect how voters are notified ahead of the August 8 special town election.

ours.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.

watch_next: Next Select Board meeting, Tuesday, July 7
Whether the detective promotion recommendation comes back for a vote

what_happened.line: The state told the Select Board electronic voting machines cannot be discontinued for the August 8 special election; they must be used.
The board ratified the Town Manager's full slate of annual town appointments by roll call, including the entire police department roster.
The board separately voted its own set of annual appointments, covering roles like Animal Control Officer and Parking Clerk.
A chief's recommendation to promote an officer to detective has not yet been taken up; that officer is listed as SRO in this round.

why_it_matters: Residents voting in the August 8 special election will use electronic voting machines, not a discontinued or alternate method, because the state ruled it mandatory.
The ratified appointments keep town officer and police department roles filled without a public vacancy or hiring process at this meeting.

ours.headline: Electronic voting machines can't be discontinued for the August special election — the state says they're mandatory.

watch_next: Select Board / Town Manager goals workshop, scheduled for July 14
Standalone dangerous/nuisance dog hearing, tentatively placeholder-planned for July 28 (may slip to August)

what_happened.line: The board voted to send state legislators a letter urging preservation of the Foundation Budget Review Commission and higher school aid in the FY27 state budget.
The board decided to hold a standalone public hearing on a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint rather than close the matter on the investigative report alone.
The group searching for a temporary food pantry site coalesced around the former School Street school, contingent on the School Committee agreeing to move T-ball off that site.
The board adopted an updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy, which will only come back for a vote when the policy itself changes.
The finance director asked to push fiscal year-end transfers between departments to July, where they still need votes from both the Select Board and Finance Committee by July 15.

why_it_matters: State school aid funds a significant share of the school budget, so the legislature's decision on the Foundation Budget Review Commission and aid levels affects how much the town has to raise locally.
The dangerous dog complaint will now get a separate public hearing, giving residents and the parties involved a formal chance to be heard before any decision.
Year-end transfers move money between town departments to cover shortfalls and require sign-off from both the Select Board and Finance Committee before the July 15 deadline.

ours.headline: The board voted to press the state legislature to preserve the Foundation Budget Review Commission and boost school aid in the FY27 budget.

watch_next: Assignment of a member-at-large and a Select Board representative to the Americans with Disabilities Committee, expected around August 2026
Applications for the remaining Conservation Committee, Cultural Council, Historical Commission and PAC vacancies

what_happened.line: The Select Board reconstituted the Personnel Committee as a five-member body and appointed three members to it.
The board also filled seats on the APDC, Council on Aging, Americans with Disabilities Committee, Conservation Committee, Cultural Council and Green Communities.
The Americans with Disabilities Committee is not expected to meet again until it has a member-at-large and a Select Board representative assigned, possibly not until August.
Vacancies remain on the Conservation Committee, Cultural Council, Historical Commission and PAC.

why_it_matters: Residents interested in serving on a town board now know which seats are filled and which -- Conservation, Cultural Council, Historical Commission, PAC -- are still open.
The Personnel Committee's reconstitution affects how the town handles personnel policy matters going forward.
A delay in staffing the Americans with Disabilities Committee could postpone its work on accessibility issues into the fall.

ours.headline: The Select Board reconstituted the Personnel Committee as a five-member body and filled its seats along with most other town board vacancies.

watch_next: August 8 special town election for two select board seats
June 15 workshop session to interview applicants for board and committee vacancies

what_happened.line: The select board set Saturday, August 8 as the date for a special town election to fill two board vacancies.
The board completed and accepted the town manager's FY26 performance evaluation, compiled by labor counsel after the board chair was unable to do so.
The board made appointments and reappointments across several committees, including the ZBA, Agricultural Commission, and cable advisory committee.
A board member urged public unity following the town's failed override vote.

why_it_matters: The August 8 special election is a vote residents will be asked to take, to fill two seats on the select board.
The town manager's annual performance evaluation is part of the town's oversight of that office, and this year it was assembled by outside labor counsel rather than the board chair.
Open seats on bodies like the Trust Fund Commission touch whether that committee can reach a quorum to act on trust fund matters.

ours.headline: Board set an August 8 special election for two vacant seats and completed the town manager's annual review

watch_next: The special-election date, once set with the town clerk
Input from the School Committee and Finance Committee on whether to call a special town meeting on the budget

what_happened.line: Vice chair Amanda Moore resigned citing health, following the failed override.
The board agreed in principle to hold a special election to fill the vacant vice-chair seat.
The board reorganized, electing a new chair 3-1 and a new vice chair and clerk unanimously.
The board held off calling a special town meeting on the budget, deferring to the School Committee and Finance Committee first.
The board voted unanimously to write off uncollectible ambulance receipts and refer the remainder to a collections agency.

why_it_matters: A vacant board seat and a leadership change affect who residents deal with on upcoming budget decisions.
Whether a special town meeting on the budget gets called determines if residents face another vote this year.
The ambulance-billing write-off is routine collections cleanup and does not by itself change any resident's tax bill.

ours.headline: Amanda Moore resigns as vice chair citing health; board reorganizes and plans a special election

watch_next: Saturday, May 16, 2026: annual town election and Proposition 2½ override vote
Town manager's annual evaluation, targeted for completion the week after the election

what_happened.line: The Select Board held its last public comment session before Saturday's override election, and the chair stated personal support for a yes vote.
The board agreed to assign a police officer rather than the elected constable to cover election day, after members raised concerns about the constable's public remarks on the override.
Residents used the session to argue over how the town split new growth revenue among capital projects, a reserve fund, a new hire, and schools.
The board voted to sell two tax-title parcels on Hollis Road, contingent on a vote by the board of assessors.
The board approved an FY27 letter to Senator Cronin urging changes to state school aid, including circuit breaker reimbursement and local aid formulas.

why_it_matters: The override goes before voters at Saturday's annual town election; the chair's public position is one member's stance, not the board's decision or the vote's outcome.

Swapping the constable for a police officer at the polls is a change to customary election-day coverage, decided informally before the formal vote and tied to the override's politics rather than a stated procedural rule.
The advocacy letter and property sale don't change any resident's tax bill directly, but the letter is the town's on-record ask for state school funding changes that could affect future budgets.

ours.headline: Select Board held final public comment on the override before Saturday's town election; the chair backed a yes vote.

watch_next: Board decision on selling or holding 250 and 356 Hollis Road, expected the following week
Board and committee recommendations, including from Open Space, on the 35 Leominster Road right of first refusal

what_happened.line: An appraisal found the 925 Mass Ave site has a negative highest-and-best-use value once remediation costs are weighed against market value, the Town Manager reported.
The board tabled a decision on the right of first refusal for 35 Leominster Road until all board and committee recommendations, including Open Space, are in.
The board also tabled whether to sell or hold the 250 and 356 Hollis Road properties for one more week to review the planning board's discussion.
The board voted unanimously to appoint Mora Lizak to the 300th Anniversary Committee and to ratify Jonathan Francis as Outreach Coordinator.
The board also approved a student civics-class art event near the library field and a small APR land lease at Lanni Orchards for shed display.

why_it_matters: The 925 Mass Ave appraisal means the town cannot count on selling the site to cover cleanup costs, so any redevelopment there likely depends on outside grants or credits.
The delayed calls on Leominster Road and the Hollis Road properties are land-use decisions that could shape future town holdings and will come back to the board rather than to voters right away.
The appointments and the Lanni Orchards lease are routine board business that residents affected by those committees or that farm property may want to track.

ours.headline: Appraisal finds the 925 Mass Ave property has a negative value, complicating the town's redevelopment plans

watch_next: Contract terms and cost figures not stated in the recording — check the ratified agreements or a future budget document for wage/benefit terms.
Whether the ratified terms appear in a future town budget or warrant article.

what_happened.line: The Select Board unanimously ratified three collective bargaining agreements, covering firefighters, municipal employees, and DPW workers.
The board discussed bargaining strategy in a closed executive session before returning to open session to vote.
No dollar figures or contract terms were stated on the record; the vote covered ratification only.
No other business was conducted, and the meeting adjourned shortly after the vote.

why_it_matters: These contracts set pay and benefit terms for three town employee groups — fire, municipal (AFSCME), and DPW (Teamsters) — which feed directly into future town budgets.
The terms themselves were not discussed in open session, so residents cannot yet see what was agreed to from this recording alone.

ours.headline: Select Board ratified three union contracts (fire, municipal employees, DPW) after executive session.

watch_next: Vote on 250 and 356 Hollis Road, held open until May 12 pending input from planning, agricultural, open space, and assessors boards
Town counsel opinion on whether the FY27 budget/override open house must be posted as an open meeting

what_happened.line: A resident used public comment to dispute claims from override supporters that the FY27 balanced budget cuts fire and police services.
The Select Board took only routine votes: a motor vehicle license, a one-day liquor license, lifeguard and beach director appointments, and a sick leave bank policy start date.
The board left open its vote on whether to sell or hold two Hollis Road parcels until May 12, to get input from other town boards first.
A second resident used public comment to promote state property-tax relief programs, tying them to the consequences of the override vote.
The board voted to enter executive session to discuss bargaining strategy for the firefighters' and AFSCME contracts.

why_it_matters: The dispute over whether the balanced budget cuts fire and police service goes to the core question residents will face on the override ballot.
The sick leave bank policy, effective July 1 with June enrollment, is a benefit change for town employees.
The Hollis Road decision affects what happens to two town-owned parcels and is not yet final.

ours.headline: Board took only routine votes; public comment sharply disputed override claims of fire and police service cuts

watch_next: Board revisit of the Hollis Road tax-title parcel decision the following week
FY27 override and warrant articles going before annual town meeting

what_happened.line: Public comment and board rebuttals covered the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and disputed newspaper coverage, but no vote was taken on the override.
The fire chief and firefighters' union president defended a proposed fourth fire shift, saying the staffing plan has not changed since last July.
The police union president disputed characterizations of town free cash as an available surplus, calling it one-time money for capital needs.
The Town Manager publicly rebutted a newspaper's article point by point on free cash, the deficit, and other disputed claims.
The board tabled a decision on selling two tax-title Hollis Road parcels until members can visit the properties.

why_it_matters: The dispute over budget figures and staffing plans bears directly on how residents weigh the FY27 override at town meeting.
Fire and police staffing levels discussed here affect emergency response coverage funded by the override.
Whether the town sells or keeps the Hollis Road parcels affects future town land use and potential revenue.

ours.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.

watch_next: Town meeting vote on Article L (FY27 budget) and Article M (override tiers)
Budget public information meeting, April 28 at the Adult Activity Center

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend the FY27 balanced budget for town meeting.
The board recommended the override's second tier by a 3-1 vote; the first tier's vote outcome was not audible on the recording.
Public commenters objected to proposed cuts to the library, senior center and beach program alongside new spending on an assistant town manager and a fourth fire shift.
The board also recommended the PAC/PEG, solid waste, water and sewer enterprise fund articles, all unanimously.
The board scheduled a budget public information meeting for the evening of April 28 at the Adult Activity Center.

why_it_matters: Both the balanced budget and the override now go to town meeting, where the choice is between a level-services budget with cuts to programs like the library, senior center and beach program, or an override that funds the assistant town manager position and a fourth fire shift.
A resident weighing the override should note the split board vote on its second tier, which signals the choice was not unanimous even among the officials recommending it.
The April 28 public information meeting is the town's forum for residents to ask about the budget and override before voting.

ours.headline: Select Board voted to send the FY27 balanced budget and both override tiers to town meeting despite sharp internal debate

watch_next: FY27 annual town meeting vote on the deferred warrant articles and the override question
The annual town election ballot, where the override appears as Question 1 and Question 2

what_happened.line: Board voted 5-0 to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, pending town counsel's final edits.
Board members individually declined to put two Trust Fund Commission articles, on legal fees and a quorum bylaw, on the town meeting warrant.
The board deferred several FY27 warrant items, including prior-year invoices and union contract funding, to town meeting itself.
A Trust Fund Commission representative told the board the commission has filed a notice of breach of fiduciary duty against the town.

why_it_matters: The override question, if it proceeds as set, will ask voters at the annual town election to approve additional property tax collection above the state cap, split into two tiers residents can vote on separately.

Sending prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, and union contract funding to town meeting itself means those costs will be settled by the voters present rather than decided in advance by the board.
The declined Trust Fund Commission articles and the fiduciary-duty notice point to an unresolved dispute between that commission and the town that may surface again at town meeting.

ours.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot

watch_next: Attorney Costa's planned presentation to the board on the trust fund commission legal fees article
Town meeting vote on the FY2027 warrant, including the override placeholder article

what_happened.line: The board voted to include most of the draft FY2027 town meeting warrant, including the Prop 2.5 override placeholder article, without recommending it.
It held off on the trust fund commission bylaw and legal-fees articles, a stormwater utility bylaw, and Central Mass Mosquito Control participation, pending legal review or more resident input.
An extended presentation on the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry operates, ended without a decision on relocation or the building's future.
The board closed a public hearing and voted unanimously to opt out of mail-in early voting for local elections this year.
The board entered executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement; that portion of the recording has no audio.

why_it_matters: Residents will see a Prop 2.5 override placeholder on the FY2027 warrant, though the board has not recommended it, so it will be a question voters take up at town meeting.
The food pantry's future home is unresolved: the board said it will not fund TC Passios roof or heating repairs without a broader plan for the building.
A handful of warrant articles -- a stormwater bylaw, mosquito control participation, and trust fund commission bylaws -- are still open and could return changed before town meeting.

ours.headline: Board included nearly all FY27 warrant articles; TC Passios' safety issues leave the food pantry's future unresolved.

watch_next: School committee's core and restoration budget numbers, due Wednesday
Town manager's restoration budget figure, due Thursday, and whether the Tri-Board meeting is rescheduled

what_happened.line: The Select Board leaned toward a two-tier override structure -- a core budget plus a separate restoration ask -- for both town and school, without taking a formal vote.

Board members worked line by line through department cuts made since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging items such as a police clerk position, a second school resource officer, fire department per diem coverage, the recreation director post, communications/IT staffing and animal control funding as candidates to restore if an override passes.

The town manager was asked to produce the town's restoration budget number by Thursday, and Thursday's planned Tri-Board meeting was flagged for cancellation or reconsideration so the school committee's core and restoration figures could come in by Wednesday instead.

The board also settled smaller line items along the way, including pursuing a town engineer position in the restoration budget regardless of storm water compliance funding and leaving the snow and ice budget unchanged rather than risk a later cut.

why_it_matters: This is the shape of the override question residents may eventually vote on -- a base town/school budget plus a separate restoration ask, rather than one combined number.
The restoration list touches police staffing, a school resource officer, fire coverage, recreation programming and animal control -- services that stay cut if no override passes.

ours.headline: Select Board leaned toward a two-tier (core + restoration) joint town/school override, no vote taken

watch_next: Whether mosquito-control funding appears as a warrant article for a town meeting vote
Final warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting, including the draft revolving-fund and capital-cleanup items reviewed this meeting

what_happened.line: The select board chair said continued funding for mosquito control should be decided by town meeting voters, not the board, amid a town budget shortfall.
No vote was taken on the mosquito control assessment; the board instead held a joint educational session with the board of health on the program.
The board approved a one-day liquor license for the Lunenburg Diner for a March 19 event.

The board reviewed, but did not vote on, draft 2026 town meeting warrant articles covering a new Economic Development revolving fund, a technology revolving fund renaming, an FY26 capital cleanup item, and vacation buyout transition language.
The board acknowledged a resignation from the Conservation Commission.

why_it_matters: If mosquito control funding goes to town meeting, residents will be asked to vote directly on whether to keep paying into that regional assessment, which a board member said the state sets using a land-mass and valuation formula rather than local choice.

The draft warrant articles reviewed -- a new revolving fund, a capital reallocation, and a policy change to vacation buyouts -- are early-stage and not yet committed to the warrant, but they preview what voters may see at the 2026 annual town meeting.
A public commenter raised a concern about pesticide safety to bees, which residents may want addressed before any funding vote.

ours.headline: Select Board leans toward letting town meeting voters decide on continued mosquito-control funding.

watch_next: Tri-board meeting tentatively set for March 10
FY27 annual town meeting warrant, where an override article would appear

what_happened.line: Board members said an FY27 override warrant article will likely go forward, with the amount and structure still undecided.
The town manager reported the budget gap identified for finance committee had narrowed after the school department adjusted its own budget.
A board member linked the likely override to both the school budget and a fire department proposal for a fourth staffing shift.
Members agreed to share blackout dates to schedule a tri-board meeting, tentatively next Tuesday, and possible budget-only workshops.
No vote was taken on an override figure or on the town's FY26 goals and objectives, which was tabled until the full board is present.

why_it_matters: An override would raise property taxes above the state levy cap and would need voter approval, likely tied to town meeting.
The size of the gap depends on decisions the school department and fire department make about their own budgets, not yet finalized.
Residents who want input should watch for the tri-board meeting and any budget-only workshops, where the override amount will start to take shape.

ours.headline: Board leans toward an FY27 override as the school/town budget gap sits near $3.15 million.

watch_next: The finalized earmark letter once the town manager adds project justifications
Action by the state legislature/delegation on the FY27 state budget earmarks

what_happened.line: Select Board voted by roll call to submit a three-item FY27 state earmark list: boiler upgrades, fire radios, primary school playground design.
The board dropped a bundled intercom/radio security request and the Fitzgerald field project after learning state guidance caps towns at one to three earmark requests.
Board ranked public safety building boiler upgrades as the top priority, ahead of fire department radios and the playground design.
The town manager will add justifications to the earmark letter and send it to all three members of the legislative delegation, not just one representative.
A separate Flat Hill supplemental budget request is being pursued by the delegation outside this earmark list.

why_it_matters: An earmark is a request for state funding outside the town's own budget, so dropping the school intercom and middle-high radio security upgrades from this list means that project now has to compete for town capital dollars instead.
The ranked order signals which project the delegation will push hardest for as the state budget moves through the legislature this session.
This affects the public safety building, the fire department, and the primary school -- not this year's town tax bill, since these are requests to the state, not town appropriations.

ours.headline: Select Board voted to submit three FY27 state earmark requests: boiler, fire radios, primary playground

watch_next: Next Select Board meeting, for the appointment policy vote with the full board present
Final school budget figures and the FY27 override question ahead of the 2026 annual town meeting

what_happened.line: The town manager told the Select Board the preliminary FY27 budget will not balance and will need an override, with the gap as heard put at more than an amount as heard pending final school figures.
Preliminary FY25 free cash is coming in well above what was budgeted, partly from a school turnback, but the capital plan still holds its lower, more conservative figure until numbers are certified.
The board spent most of the meeting revising its FY26 goals line by line and reviewing warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting, deferring the appointment policy vote to the next meeting.
Three routine items passed unanimously: a Common Victualer license for Empire Athletics, ratifying a payroll and benefits coordinator appointment, and declaring an old stove surplus.

why_it_matters: An override signal this early means residents should expect a tax-related vote tied to the FY27 budget once school figures are finalized.
Free cash running above the budgeted assumption could fund one-time costs like the snow and ice deficit or stabilization reserves, but the town manager is not yet building it into the capital plan.
The warrant articles and goals decided at this meeting shape what residents will see and vote on at the 2026 annual town meeting.

ours.headline: Town manager says the preliminary FY27 budget won't balance and will need an override, projected over $3 million short

watch_next: Storm water utility public information session, March 5, library, 6:30-8:00 p.m.
Warrant article submission deadline for other boards/committees, March 16

what_happened.line: Board and Planning Board heard a joint presentation on a proposed storm water utility bylaw and fee for spring Town Meeting, with mixed public reaction on cost and HOA road applicability.
Board ratified two new police sergeants and formed a cable advisory committee to begin Comcast contract renewal talks.
Town manager reported on FY27 budget preparation and said the town cancelled its ClearGov budgeting software subscription over cost and staffing constraints.
Board asked the town manager to bring the Board of Health and a mosquito-control program presentation back before deciding whether to drop that assessment from a warrant article.
A family repeated allegations of town retaliation tied to a records request about a payment to a homeowners association, unresolved for a second time this meeting.

why_it_matters: The storm water utility, if adopted at spring Town Meeting, would likely appear as a separate fee rather than folded into the tax-funded operating budget, and a board member compared that fee against what an override for the same cost would mean per household.
Cutting the Central Mass Mosquito Control assessment from the FY27 warrant is now an open question the town manager will bring back with input from the Board of Health.
The cancelled ClearGov subscription and the FY27 budget prep discussion touch how the town builds and explains next year's budget to residents.

ours.headline: Board reviewed a proposed storm water utility fee bylaw headed to spring Town Meeting, split public reaction

watch_next: February 13th: DLS deadline for the FY25 Schedule A, or confirmation of an extension
March 16th: deadline for boards and committees to submit warrant articles for town meeting

what_happened.line: The town manager told the Select Board that FY27 cost drivers are outpacing revenue growth and an override may be needed absent service cuts.
The town has not filed its FY25 Schedule A with the state, and missing the February 13th deadline risks the state withholding local aid; an extension is being sought.
Free cash remains uncertified, which affects town meeting planning including the capital plan and the snow-and-ice deficit.
The board voted unanimously to retain Labor Counsel Mark Terry under his new firm and approved two peddler's licenses.
A joint warrant article on the Kids Kingdom relocation was proposed, and other boards were given a March 16th deadline to submit warrant articles.

why_it_matters: An FY27 override, if pursued, would come before voters and would raise property taxes above the state levy limit.
A late or unfiled FY25 Schedule A risks the state withholding local aid, a funding source that supports both town and school budgets.
Uncertified free cash limits how much the town can commit at town meeting to capital projects, reserve transfers, and covering this winter's snow-and-ice deficit.
