30 Summer Street hearing continues May 6, 2026

what_happened.line: The commission approved DPW's Northville Crossing culvert replacement after a years-long right-of-entry delay was resolved.
Four continued hearings on a Parmenter/Round Road subdivision drew resident questions about wetland impact, runoff, and rain-garden maintenance before being pushed to April 15.
A years-long unpermitted clearing violation near Mass Ave was resolved with an accepted planting and phasing plan rather than a formal violation filing.
A proposed multi-year herbicide treatment plan for Marshall Pond was continued to April 15 pending a state DEP file number.
A proposed stormwater utility bylaw was held back from this town meeting cycle given the town's broader budget pressures.

why_it_matters: The culvert approval clears a long-stalled DPW infrastructure project that affects drainage at Northville Crossing.
The Parmenter/Round Road subdivision hearings, and residents' runoff and well-water questions, will keep returning to this board through at least mid-April as more lots move toward permits.
Holding the stormwater utility bylaw back this cycle means any new fee or funding mechanism for stormwater management is delayed to a future town meeting, not decided now.

ours.headline: Commission approved DPW's Northville Crossing culvert replacement after a years-long right-of-entry delay was resolved.

watch_next: April 1, 2026 meeting -- continued hearings for Hickory Hills, Catales, DPW culvert, Safe Store, and the 314 Highland Street violation
April 15, 2026 -- continued NOI hearing for 922 Flat Hill Road

what_happened.line: The commission found unpermitted tree removals at multiple properties, including one already under review for a driveway violation.
Four pending hearings -- an ADA dock/ramp, a new home, an addition, and a culvert replacement -- were continued to April for missing storm-water calculations, revised plans, or a site walk.
The commission ratified, 4-0, an administrative determination allowing four dead trees to be cut at 100 Hemlock Road, with stumps left for slope stability.
A formal violation and fine for tree removal at 314 Highland Street was held off pending the property owner's appearance at the April 1 meeting.
A budget update for the land use/conservation office, combined with land use, was deferred about a month.

why_it_matters: Unpermitted tree removal and drainage violations found this meeting could lead to fines or required plantings at several private properties once hearings resume in April.
Four active building and infrastructure projects -- a beach dock, a new home, an addition, and a DPW culvert -- remain paused, affecting nearby residents and applicants awaiting permits.
A stormwater utility, discussed as a possible new fee collected like the sewer bill, is being explored town-wide to fund drainage infrastructure.

ours.headline: Commission found unpermitted tree removals at several properties and continued four hearings to April

watch_next: April 1, 2026 continued hearing on the New Westminster Road townhouse subdivision's driveway
Town counsel's response on relocating the conservation fee schedule into a bylaw

what_happened.line: Commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a chapter 61 forestry parcel at 1083 Northfield Road, letting the pending sale proceed.
An applicant withdrew a request to amend wetlands conditions at 50 Pine Grove Road after the hearing was found improperly noticed, and will refile with proper notice.
The conservation agent will consult town counsel about moving the fee schedule out of the town charter and into a commission bylaw, and about billing for items not currently charged.
A proposed 20-unit townhouse subdivision's common driveway on New Westminster Road was continued to April 1 while other wetlands filings were approved with conditions or continued for site walks.
Members noted that grants requiring a local match have relied on tree-harvesting revenue from conservation land, and said a replacement funding source needs planning if that revenue drops.

why_it_matters: Declining the right of first refusal means the town gives up its option to buy or steer the future use of the chapter 61 land before it changes private hands.
Moving the fee schedule into a standalone bylaw and billing for administrative approvals, amendments, and certificates could raise the cost of routine wetlands filings for residents.
The revenue the commission uses to match conservation grants comes from harvesting on town conservation land, a source members flagged as needing a backup plan.

ours.headline: Commission voted not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on a chapter 61 forestry parcel

30 Summer Street flood-plain fill hearing continues March 18, 2026

what_happened.line: Last year's whole-lake herbicide treatment at Lake Shirley suppressed invasive fanwort but caused a bigger-than-expected drop in native plants and water clarity, the annual report found.
The commission accepted Commissioner Chris St. Germaine's resignation and then voted to add him back as an associate member, pending town manager approval.
The board approved a septic repair, a detached garage, and a patio reconstruction, while continuing hearings on a flood-plain fill project, a culvert replacement, and a house rebuild.
The agent proposed moving the town's outdated conservation fee schedule out of the town charter and into the conservation bylaw so the commission could set fees itself, without a town meeting vote.
A committee update described a proposed residential stormwater utility fee, with commercial properties charged based on their impervious surface area.

why_it_matters: The Lake Shirley plant and clarity data will inform whether the town pursues another herbicide treatment, which affects lake recreation and future treatment costs.
Shifting the fee schedule into the bylaw would let the commission raise conservation permit fees on its own rather than bringing changes to town meeting for a vote.
A stormwater utility fee, if it advances, would show up as a new charge on residential and commercial property owners tied to impervious surface area.

ours.headline: Lake Shirley's whole-lake herbicide treatment killed invasive fanwort but also cut native plants and clarity

Four pending wetlands and flood-plain hearings were continued to February 18, including a contested request to waive a no-build zone for a larger replacement house at 27 Fire Road.
A hearing on the town DPW's proposed culvert replacement at 763 Northfield Road was also continued to February 18.
The commission is holding off on revamping its fee structure and consultant fees until the new conservation agent starts on February 9.

why_it_matters: The dam-safety tree removal affects the shoreline around Hickory Hills Lake and comes with a replanting condition rather than leaving the area bare.
The 27 Fire Road no-build-zone waiver, still undecided, will shape how close a rebuilt house can sit to protected wetland; abutters and the applicant return February 18.
A revised commission fee structure could change what applicants pay for wetlands review once the new conservation agent is in place.

watch_next: Next Conservation Commission meeting: February 4, 2026 -- 30 Summer Street and 27 Fire Road hearings resume
58 Spring Street Extension hearing continued to February 18, 2026

Three pending hearings -- 58 Spring Street, 30 Summer Street, and 27 Fire Road -- were continued after applicants' engineers said plans or materials were not yet ready.
A DPW notice of intent for work at 763 Northville Road was also continued to a later date.
The Commission approved a purchase order for heating oil at the town-owned Hollis Road residence so bills can be paid without a vote each time.
Members discussed moving the bylaw's consulting-engineering peer-review cost language into regulations instead, without resolving it.

why_it_matters: Committing Timber Rights Fund money as the grant match ties that fund to the Table Rock and Raino Road trail-parking projects going forward.
Residents near Lake Shirley and along Summer Street and Fire Road with pending building or floodplain work will see their cases decided at later hearings, not this one.
A possible move of engineering peer-review costs from the bylaw into regulations would change how those costs are set for future applicants without going back through a bylaw amendment.

ours.headline: Commission voted to submit two trail-parking grant applications and commit Timber Rights Fund money as the match.

Snow-dog grooming was approved for a year on the Lane property and Large Town Forest, but only on mapped trails, not private land.

The commission agreed to add a buffer-zone information flyer as a budgeted line item for the coming fiscal year, cost still to be quoted.

why_it_matters: Trail users, including hikers, skiers and snowmobilers, gain a defined grooming season but only on town-mapped routes, not adjoining private land.
Property owners with pending wetlands or tree-removal applications near Spring Street, Summer Street, Northfield Road and Fire Road 15A will see those cases return January 21.
A conservation-agent staffing change and a proposed mailing flyer are small additions that could show up in next year's conservation budget line.

A future agenda item on the long-term use of the Hollis Road residence.

Four wetlands hearings -- Mopus Road, Summer Street, a Northfield Road culvert, and Fire Road 15A -- were continued to January 7 for more information.
The Commission voted to cover Hollis Road property costs from the Hollis fund, including a heating-service contract, back bills, and a remote monitoring device for the vacant building.
The order of conditions for Zero Shirley Reservoir Road was extended to August 2029 ahead of the project going to bid.
Members discussed moving the bylaw's consultant-fee cap into an easier-to-change regulation rather than the bylaw itself.

why_it_matters: Anyone using the Town Forest's mountain-bike trails will see grooming paused until a plan is on file, a condition tied to volunteer maintenance work residents praised in public comment.
The four continued hearings mean the property owners at those addresses face another wait before any wetlands permit is decided.
The town-owned Hollis Road property is now drawing recurring costs from its dedicated fund, and its longer-term use is set to come back as a full agenda item.

The conservation agent job was reclassified out of the clerical union, and the commission voted a new budget split favoring materials for Hollis property cleanup.

why_it_matters: Anyone planning a structure near wetlands should note the 50-foot no-structure zone is being enforced strictly, even for additions like a porch.
The reclassified conservation agent position changes how the town staffs and pays for wetland permit review going forward.
Applicants and abutters tied to the Mulpus Road, Summer Street, and Northfield Road projects face another hearing before a decision is reached.

It issued negative determinations with conditions for a well-drilling request near Lake Shirley and a fence request at 40 Hemlock Drive.
A shed request near a stream at 480 Mopus Road was continued so the agent can field-verify where the buffer line actually falls.
The commission found that a well-abandonment notice for a Massachusetts Ave gas station site does not qualify for the exemption claimed and must instead be formally filed.
The town's DPW culvert replacement over Mulpus Brook on Northfield Road was also continued to December 3.

why_it_matters: The 30 Summer Street case decides whether a self-storage conversion can fill flood-plain land, a use question that outlasts this one hearing.
Wetlands rulings on wells, fences and sheds set the conditions individual property owners near water or in buffer zones must follow before building.
The disputed exemption claim and the delayed culvert project both touch town infrastructure and permitting decisions residents may later see cost or timeline effects from.

why_it_matters: The 199 Mass Ave case will decide how a wetland-buffer violation gets enforced, and construction there stays paused until the commission takes it up again.
The Lake Shirley and Lake Wham approvals set the conditions those shoreline owners must follow, including work timing tied to the lake draw-down.
Closing out the 215 Sunset Lane complaint without a vote ends that runoff matter near Hickory Hills Lake with no formal record of the decision.

The continued culvert hearing affects the timeline for a DPW infrastructure project crossing Mulpus Brook, now set for November 5.

A certificate of compliance for 155 Reservoir Road was denied for lack of a stamped as-built plan.

why_it_matters: The driveway approval sets wetland-protection conditions for a four-lot residential project, with two years of required monitoring.
Homeowners proposing tree removal, decks or docks near wetlands may be routed into the longer, costlier RDA review depending on how much ground work is involved.
Closing out a wetlands permit requires a stamped as-built plan on file; without one, the compliance certificate can be denied even after work is finished.

why_it_matters: Property owners with pending applications at 560 Mulpus Road, 809 Chase Road, and 1083 Northfield Road will not get a final decision until the September 17 hearing.
The tree-replacement condition at 44 Hemlock Terrace is the kind of standard the commission can apply to future tree-removal requests.

Two hearings were continued to September 3: Ashley Owens's 68A Laurel Lane project, missing its NOI number, and Tanner Cole's common driveway, pending peer review.
The Commission also approved several driveway, septic, wall, deck and tree-removal projects in wetland buffer zones, and issued negative determinations for a well and a deck project.
Two certificates of compliance and one tree-removal request were left unresolved, pending agent follow-up or a site visit before the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The Lake Wham approval sets a five-year plan for herbicide use near the town beach, with notice to residents handled through the town website and social media rather than a mailed abutter list.
Wetland buffer-zone approvals for driveways, septic systems, walls and tree removal show how the Commission conditions rather than blocks routine residential projects near water.
Two properties (68A Laurel Lane, Tanner Cole's driveway) and two certificates of compliance remain undecided, affecting those owners' pending work.

Members discussed gaps in tracking multi-year follow-up conditions on approved projects in the town's permitting software, with no fix decided.

why_it_matters: This covers wetlands permitting near lakes and residential lots -- decisions that set conditions landowners must follow before building or altering land near protected areas.
Commissioners raised recurring concerns about one delineation firm's wetland-flagging accuracy, which affects how reliably nearby projects' buffer and boundary conditions are set.
A gap in tracking required follow-up inspections (like plant-survival checks) means some approved conditions may go unverified as town staff turn over.

page.overview:
The Conservation Commission is a seven-member commission, the members of which are appointed to staggered three-year terms by the Select Board. The Conservation Commission enforces the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act and the Lunenburg Wetlands Protection By-law. The Commission also has care and custody of over 24 publicly accessible properties that are permanently protected for conservation and passive recreation.
VOLUNTEERS NEEDED
Conservation Commission seeks 1 Member
To apply, Please go to our Serve on a Board or Committee page, OR please reach out to Melissa Richard

watch_next: Next Council on Aging meeting: review of the policies and procedures packet before it is reposted online
The parking lot capital planning request as it moves into the town's capital budget process

what_happened.line: Council on Aging agreed to seek capital-plan funding for a parking lot redesign at the senior center.
Board decided to write its own entry for the town report, separate from the director's operational report.
Board turned down joining a multi-town "friendly neighbors" program and will instead expand its own friendly visitors program.
Director will send the board the FY26 year-end financial report after confusion over the current gift fund balance.
Chair will ask whether Lunenburg can be added to the ambulance catchment area of a new UMass emergency facility in Groton.

why_it_matters: A capital-plan request puts the senior center parking lot and ADA access into the town's capital budget process, where it will compete with other town projects for funding.
The gift fund balance confusion and the push for regular financial reports touch how residents can track money donated to the Council on Aging.
Whether Lunenburg joins the new Groton facility's EMS catchment area could affect ambulance response for seniors and others in town.

ours.headline: Council on Aging agreed to pursue a capital-plan funding request for the senior center's parking lot redesign

watch_next: The director's draft gift-fund policy, to come back for board approval
The September financial report, which the board will use to decide on any FY26 fund reallocation

what_happened.line: The board asked the director to draft a written policy for the COA gift fund, which currently has no procedure governing how it can be spent.
The FY27 department budget was read aloud, covering programs, training and supplies, but the figure does not include salaries.
Members noted the outreach coordinator position sat vacant for part of the year, and a transfer from that salary line to office supplies had already been made.
The board urged seniors to file for the means-tested tax exemption and circuit breaker credit before the deadline.
Funding for the September honorary-member luncheon was left to the director's discretion, with the board leaning toward voluntary member contributions rather than a program or meal account.

why_it_matters: The gift fund is money donated to the Council on Aging, and the absence of a written approval procedure means there is currently no documented rule for how the board authorizes its use.
Seniors who qualify can combine the elderly exemption and the circuit breaker credit to reduce a property tax bill, but only if they file by the deadline the board flagged.
Moving unspent salary money to cover office supplies is a within-department transfer the board discussed doing again before any leftover FY26 funds revert to the town's general fund.

ours.headline: Board urges seniors to apply for tax exemptions by the deadline; flags no written policy for its own gift fund

watch_next: Committee's findings on whether to join the Village to Village / Mishoba Neighbors network
Ratification of the new outreach coordinator hire

what_happened.line: Board members privately arranged two pavilion band concerts after the failed override ended town-funded band concerts.
The board agreed to explore forming a committee on a regional volunteer-matching model for housebound seniors, weighing its fee schedule.
Two new board members were formally welcomed and seated.
The director reported no funds spent yet this fiscal year; unspent COA money reverts to the town's general fund at year end.
A friendly visitor volunteer training session was scheduled for late July.

why_it_matters: Town-sponsored band concerts ended when the override failed; this summer's shows happened only because board members paid for them privately, with no guarantee for future years.
Pursuing the volunteer-matching network under consideration would mean a new recurring membership cost for the Council on Aging, which is only being explored, not yet decided.
COA funds not spent by year end return to the town's general fund rather than carrying over, a mechanism worth knowing when reading the department's year-end totals.

ours.headline: COA privately funds two summer concerts after override cut town band; explores senior outreach networks.

watch_next: A draft letter to the Select Board on mail-in balloting for homebound seniors, from the new subcommittee
The next meeting, when the director is expected to clarify gift fund and Eagle House Supporters fund policy

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging board voted to form a subcommittee to petition the Select Board and town clerk for mail-in ballots for homebound seniors.
The board elected its chair and vice chair for the coming year.
The board amended its honorary-member policy and nominated a new honorary member, its third.
A question over whether a large donation belongs to the COA gift fund or the separate Eagle House Supporters fund was tabled until the director can weigh in.
The chair said the financial report given to the board lacked the account and grant-balance detail requested and asked for more detail next time.

why_it_matters: A subcommittee pushing for mail-in ballots for homebound seniors could affect how those residents vote in future town elections, pending Select Board and town clerk action.
Unresolved confusion between the COA gift fund and the Eagle House Supporters fund means donors and the board itself are currently unclear which fund a gift lands in and what policy governs it.
A caregiver fee at the veterans breakfast was changed without the board being informed, which the board flagged as a gap in oversight of day-to-day COA policy changes going forward.

ours.headline: COA forms a subcommittee to push the Select Board for mail-in ballots for homebound seniors

watch_next: The override ballot question vote on May 16
The bylaws subcommittee's revised clerk-appointment language, expected in the fall

what_happened.line: Town meeting approved the appropriations for both tiers of the proposed override; a ballot question on May 16 decides whether either, both, or neither takes effect.
A resident's letter, read into the record, warned the override would force cuts to paid help and grocery delivery for a homebound senior.
The board nominated and approved David Lincoln as chair and Lou Franco as vice chair, effective July 1.
Colleen Roy's application was accepted to fill one of two open board seats after Helen Bolkum's departure.
The bylaws subcommittee will propose removing the sentence on clerk appointment and bring the bylaws back in the fall.

why_it_matters: The May 16 override ballot question determines town funding levels, and this board heard direct testimony that a yes vote could mean cuts to services homebound seniors rely on.
A change in board chair and vice chair, plus a new member filling a vacancy, will shape how the Council on Aging is run starting July 1.
Continuing uncertainty over who takes board minutes reflects a staffing gap the town manager and board have not yet resolved.

ours.headline: Board nominates new chair/vice chair for July as a resident's letter warns the override will hurt homebound seniors

watch_next: The special town meeting vote on the override article
Whether the 41A deferral program is restored to the town website and handout materials are produced

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging director reported the 41A property tax deferral program has disappeared from the town website's exemptions listing, weeks before the override vote.
The board urged seniors to attend the upcoming special town meeting and discussed what an override would mean for residents on fixed incomes.
Members voted to have a board member and a resident explore next steps and funding for a donated playground and parking-lot redesign.
The board voted to set case-by-case criteria for honorary Council on Aging membership, then voted to award one to Pete Lincoln.
The board decided to get the 41A deferral program corrected on the town website and produce handout material ahead of the override vote.

why_it_matters: The 41A deferral lets eligible seniors put off paying part of their property tax bill, and its disappearance from the town's own listing could leave residents facing a higher override bill unaware the option exists.
Seniors on fixed incomes are the group most exposed to an override's effect on the tax bill, which is why the board is pressing attendance at the special town meeting where the override is decided.

The playground and parking-lot redesign draws on funds already set aside at a prior town meeting, so its progress depends on a design estimate and possible added grant funding, not a new appropriation.

ours.headline: COA found the 41A property tax deferral program missing from the town website weeks before the override vote

watch_next: Next Council on Aging meeting: finalized honorary membership criteria and a vote on the nominated honorary member
Status update on the caregiver resource connection program once the responsible staff member returns

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging reported hiring a new full-time outreach worker, starting March 23.
The board deferred finalizing honorary membership criteria to its next meeting, after nominating a past chair for the honor.
The director asked the town manager to raise the center's programming budget line to match increases given to the library.
The board agreed to let seniors sponsor another senior's cost on program and trip sign-up forms.
The caregiver resource connection program update was tabled pending the return of the staff member who oversees it.

why_it_matters: A new full-time outreach position affects the town's personnel budget and the level of direct service the senior center can offer residents.
A request to raise the center's programming line is a budget ask that would need town approval and affects funding parity across departments.
The sponsor-a-senior option and the tabled caregiver program both touch how accessible center services are to residents who need them most.

ours.headline: Council on Aging hired a new full-time outreach worker and began setting rules for honorary board membership.

watch_next: Bylaws subcommittee's first meeting, Thursday, using examples from other towns
Board members return with criteria for an honorary/emeritus member status at a future meeting

what_happened.line: The council agreed to send a letter of support for the caregiver reform legislation the two state representatives are sponsoring.
Representatives Kushmerick and Scarsdale said delegation earmarks helped cover part of last year's school budget gap through direct funding.
The council limited its role in a proposed seniors-reading-to-students program to organizing volunteer readers, not addressing school reading proficiency.
A board member pressed the delegation to shift more state aid into the flexible unrestricted general government category instead of separate restricted grants.

why_it_matters: The caregiver bill and grant-versus-flexible-aid debate touch how state money reaches senior services and the town's general budget, not just this board.

ours.headline: State Reps Kushmerick and Scarsdale briefed the COA on caregiver legislation, grants, and school/healthcare funding fights.

watch_next: Next Council on Aging meeting: HR update on the assistant director/outreach coordinator job description
Bylaw review committee's research and proposed rewrite of the Council on Aging bylaw

what_happened.line: Board members individually voiced support for pairing seniors with elementary students, but took no formal vote since the item was not on the agenda.
The board voted to take over producing its own meeting minutes, using AI transcription or volunteers, to ease strain on short-staffed Senior Center personnel.
The Senior Center director reported the district superintendent has expressed interest in developing an intergenerational senior-school program.
Staff will check with HR on the status of an assistant director job description ahead of the next meeting.
The board's own bylaw will go to the bylaw review committee for a rewrite, as it appears outdated and possibly inconsistent with the town-manager form of government.

why_it_matters: A senior-school pairing program would touch both school staffing and student achievement, but it has not been formally proposed, voted on, or agendized by either body.
How the Council on Aging documents its own meetings is changing, which affects public access to the board's record going forward.
A bylaw rewrite could change how the Council on Aging is structured and how it relates to the town-manager form of government.

ours.headline: COA informally backs pairing seniors with students in schools; board takes over minute-taking to ease staff load

watch_next: Town Manager's research on the assistant director position's cost and job description
Select Board consideration of Article 12 with the COA Chair present

what_happened.line: Board voted to have the Town Manager research creating a new assistant director position, its cost and duties.
Board separately voted to urge hiring a replacement for the departing outreach coordinator without delay.
Board voted to have its Chair represent the Council on Aging before the Select Board on Article 12, town warrant notification.
Bylaws feedback and a lobby-furnishings purchase were tabled to a later meeting.

why_it_matters: A new assistant director position would add a funded town staff role, a decision that can affect future budget requests and, members noted, could bear on a future property tax override.
Voting to fill the departing coordinator's post separately from the study means senior outreach services continue while the larger staffing question is researched.
Article 12 concerns how the town posts and notifies residents of town meeting warrants, and now goes to the Select Board with the COA Chair representing the board's position.

ours.headline: Board voted to study creating an assistant director role while pushing ahead to fill Pauline's departing post

watch_next: That evening's town meeting vote on electronic-only warrant distribution.
December 1 deadline for COA comments on hiring-participation charter language.

what_happened.line: Members voiced opposition to the town's plan to stop mailing warrants and go electronic-only, without taking a formal vote, ahead of that night's town meeting.
The board agreed to send the master plan committee a list of senior needs covering assisted living, tax relief, parking, staffing, meals, walkability, and programs.
New lobby furniture was approved, to be paid mostly from the director's gift fund with grant money covering the remainder.
The board recommended adding positions to the personnel plan administratively rather than eliminating positions through the town meeting budget, to preserve flexibility.
Review of charter language on COA participation in hiring the center director was deferred pending more information from the select board and town manager.

why_it_matters: Ending mailed warrants would change how residents, including seniors without internet access, learn what is on a town meeting warrant.
The needs list submitted to the master plan committee can shape future town funding decisions on senior transportation, meals, facilities, and programming.
Whether staff changes go through administrative reclassification or a town meeting budget vote affects both the board's flexibility and job security for center employees.

ours.headline: Board informally opposed the town's move to mail-free warrants ahead of that night's town meeting vote

watch_next: Board feedback on the Article 3 bylaw revision, due Dec. 2
Next meeting: staffing/reorganization proposal brought to the full board

what_happened.line: A town-drafted rewrite of Article 3 would fold the COA director's duties into the board's own charge; the board held it for review and asked for the director's job description to compare against it.
The board ratified its earlier vote authorizing work with the town on a 41A tax-deferral article for town meeting, unanimously.
The director presented the COA's FY27 budget request as part of a joint tri-board review with the finance committee, school committee and select board.
The board told the director to bring any assistant-director/program-coordinator restructuring ideas to the full board before taking them to the tri-board in the future.
A vote to let the director keep pursuing grant-funding opportunities with the town was recorded, but the outcome was not audible in the recording.

why_it_matters: A bylaw change to who runs the senior center's day-to-day duties is up for board feedback before a Dec. 2 deadline, and residents who use COA programs may want to weigh in.
The 41A article would widen who qualifies to defer property tax, a mechanism some senior households use to put off a tax bill until a home is sold.
The COA's FY27 budget request is part of the town's tri-board process that ultimately shapes the property tax rate voters see.

ours.headline: Town-proposed bylaw rewrite would blend the COA director's duties into the board's; feedback due by Dec. 2

watch_next: The board member's presentation on the senior building-permit fee waiver, due back to this board before it goes to the select board
The distribution formula and per-town amount for state aid to communities affected by the area hospital closure, once released

what_happened.line: A board member said the district ended FY25 with a large share of its override-funded budget unspent, calling it something residents on both sides should question.
The board voted to authorize a member to keep working on a senior property tax exemption under state statute 41A.
A board member proposed waiving building permit fees for seniors on small jobs and will bring a presentation back to the board before seeking select board approval.
The board agreed to tell the town's master planning process that an assisted-living facility should be a "must have" given the area's loss of medical facilities.
Senior center hours will revert to an earlier weekday closing time from November through February, with only Wednesday evenings staying open late.

why_it_matters: The unspent-funds comment raises a question about how override money approved by voters for the schools was actually used in FY25 -- the school budget vs. actual spending is a separate accounting question this board did not itself resolve.

The 41A vote keeps alive a path toward property tax relief for qualifying seniors, and the proposed permit fee waiver would touch town permit revenue and senior services if it advances to the select board.
The push for assisted-living to count as a "must have" in the master plan, and the seasonal cut to senior center hours, both affect what services and facilities seniors in town can expect.

ours.headline: Board member says school district left ~$600,000 of the override-funded FY25 budget unspent

watch_next: Committee members' senior-needs ideas for the master plan, due by October 1
September meeting decision on trial Friday/evening hours; the 41A warrant article draft

what_happened.line: Installing an elevator at the senior center was ruled out as infeasible on space, code and cost grounds; porch screening was raised as a cheaper alternative but not decided.
The committee agreed to seek member ideas for a 10-year senior needs section of the town's master plan, due back by October 1.

The board agreed to draft a warrant article asking the town to formally adopt the 41A property tax deferral program, after a resident reportedly lost a deferral this year because the town has not formally approved it.
The chair agreed to draft a letter about a resident's complaint over Unitil's solar-interconnection fees, to be sent once the select board liaison returns to sign on.
A decision on making trial Friday closures and evening hours permanent was postponed to the September meeting.

why_it_matters: The elevator decision affects whether the senior center becomes more accessible to residents with mobility limitations, and what replaces it will need its own funding and approval.
The 41A warrant article, if it advances, would give seniors a formal, town-approved way to defer property taxes rather than relying on inconsistent practice.
The master plan's senior needs section and the assisted-living goal will shape what the town commits to planning for seniors over the next decade.

ours.headline: Senior center elevator project ruled out as infeasible; committee to seek input on 10-year senior needs plan

watch_next: The one-page fee-waiver proposal (age threshold, construction-value cap, list of repairs requiring permits), due back to the council before going to the building commissioner and Select Board
Next Council on Aging meeting, August 12, 2025

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging is drafting a plan to waive building permit fees for qualifying seniors on small home repairs, to go next to the building commissioner and Select Board; no vote was taken.
A member asked how many permits are issued each year and how much fee revenue a waiver would cost the town, but no figures were available yet.
The council held off printing new kiosk artwork because a kitchen-staffing crunch could change who or what the panel should show.
A member reported a resident's property tax deferral application succeeded after a bank initially resisted the required lien.
The council moved its next meeting to August 12.

why_it_matters: Qualifying seniors doing small home repairs could eventually see their building permit fee reduced or waived, a change the Select Board -- not town meeting -- would set.
The town has not yet estimated how much permit revenue a senior fee waiver would forgo, a gap the proposal's drafter flagged as needed before it can move forward.
The property tax deferral program lets eligible seniors put off paying their tax bill, with interest accruing until the property is sold or transferred, rather than paying it that year.

ours.headline: Council weighs waiving building permit fees for seniors on small home repairs; no vote taken

watch_next: Results of the lift feasibility/architectural study
Evaluation of the extended-hours trial after September, and the FY27 budget proposal

what_happened.line: Board voted to commission a feasibility study for a lift to reach unused upstairs rooms at Eagle House.
Board agreed to trial extended building hours -- more evenings, fewer Friday afternoons -- through at least September rather than vote on it outright.
FY27 budget planning flagged a possible full-time recreation director and new outreach and program-coordinator roles.
Board postponed a decision on entry-seating furniture, agreeing to look for a compromise between two options.
Board approved its officer slate for the coming year and thanked two retiring longtime members.

why_it_matters: A capital study for an elevator or lift is a step toward a construction project that would need town funding and a building-committee process before any work happens.
A trial of building hours changes when seniors can use Eagle House's programs and services, ahead of any permanent change.
Proposed new staff roles and a full-time recreation director would show up as line items in the FY27 town budget residents vote on at town meeting.

ours.headline: Board voted to study installing a small lift to reach unused upstairs rooms at Eagle House.

watch_next: August capital plan: elevator/accessibility study for the senior center
FY27 budget request: program coordinator position and assistant director title change

what_happened.line: The board voted to oppose converting Memorial Drive into a permanent green space, citing parking and safety at the senior and teen centers.
FY26 moved two KitchenAide positions and the meal site manager into the town budget while a part-time outreach coordinator position was lost.
For FY27 the director will request a new program coordinator and a title change from outreach coordinator to assistant director.
An elevator/accessibility study for the building's older section is set to go into the town's August capital plan.

why_it_matters: The Memorial Drive vote is a position the board is putting on record ahead of any town decision on the parcel's use.
Moving positions from grant to town funding, and losing others, changes what the senior center budget line covers going forward.
The FY27 staffing requests and the capital-plan elevator study are items that will come before the town for funding.

ours.headline: COA voted to formally oppose turning Memorial Drive into green space, citing parking and safety impacts.

watch_next: Whether the facilities department includes the second-floor elevator/lift study in the FY27 capital plan
The next COA meeting, where the senior healthcare advocacy team proposal returns with concrete ideas

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging voted to ask the town's facilities department to add a feasibility study for elevator or lift access to the Eagle House's second floor to the FY27 capital plan.
The director laid out FY27 staffing requests: a meal-site funding buffer, a new program coordinator position, and an upgraded assistant-director/outreach title with a raise.
FY26 budget review showed the COA losing a part-time outreach assistant position while adding two kitchen aide positions and a full-time meal site manager.
The board amended its prior minutes to describe fire department coverage as "on-call firefighters" rather than volunteers before the minutes go to town hall.
The board set aside a proposed senior healthcare advocacy team, agreeing to return with concrete ideas at the next meeting rather than act now.

why_it_matters: A capital-plan request for an elevator or lift study is an early step that would need to survive the town's FY27 capital budgeting process before any accessibility work at the senior center happens.
The FY27 staffing and program requests -- a program coordinator, a retitled assistant-director role with a raise, and meal-program funding -- would draw on the town budget residents vote on.
The FY26 staffing changes show how the meal program and outreach work are currently being covered, which bears on how the FY27 requests are judged.

ours.headline: COA votes to request a second-floor elevator/lift feasibility study for the FY27 town capital plan

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Cultural Council is responsible for disbursing funds received from the Massachusetts Cultural Council for local cultural and artistic activities.
The mission of the Lunenburg Cultural Council is to nurture and promote a diverse range of artistic and cultural programs for the benefit of Lunenburg and surrounding communities.
We accomplish this through the annual allocation of state grants for local projects and by producing cultural events using locally-raised funds.
The Council reviews proposals and grants funds to local applicants for a variety of projects that benefit Lunenburg citizens. Local Cultural Councils support community-based projects in the arts, sciences, and humanities every year. The state legislature provides an annual appropriation to the Massachusetts Cultural Council, a state agency, which then allocates funds to each community.
The Lunenburg Cultural Council recognizes that the arts, humanities, and interpretive sciences form an important part of Lunenburg's history, identity, and vision. We are committed to nurturing our artistic community through supporting events that are accessible, collaborative, and fun for Lunenburg residents and visitors of all ages.

Town counsel confirmed non-restaurant businesses, such as a nail salon, can let customers bring their own alcohol without town permission.
Leominster's economic development coordinator briefed the committee on that city's marketing, sponsorship, and small-business grant programs.

How this committee defines its own charge affects what economic development work Lunenburg pursues going forward, and that decision is on hold pending a hire outside the committee's control.

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is being formed by the Planning Board in order to better assist, counsel, and advise the residents of Lunenburg, the Planning Board, other Town Boards and Departments, and Lunenburg businesses on ways to promote the local economy.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is committed to promoting business development that will enhance the character, culture, and commerce in Lunenburg. The Committee shall investigate current economic conditions to provide advice to Town Departments on economic development policy; meet and work with current Lunenburg businesses and prospective businesses; coordinate its activities with the appropriate Town Boards and Commissions; and work cooperatively with businesses and state agencies to retain, develop and promote businesses in Lunenburg.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of five regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Planning Board as follows: One member recommended by the Agricultural Commission that owns a business in Lunenburg and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Open Space Committee and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Conservation Commission and shall initially be appointed for a two-year term; Two members that are residents of Lunenburg, one shall initially be appointed for a two-year term and one shall initially be appointed for a one year term. In addition to the regular members, there will be four ex-officio members as follows: One member of the Select Board chosen annually by the Select Board; One member of the Planning Board chosen annually by the Planning Board; The Director of Planning and Economic Development; and A Lunenburg Business Owner.
After the initial term, all members shall serve a three-year term.
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power; ex-officio members shall not have the power to vote.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee and the Planning Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The Committee shall keep a recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. This charge may be amended at any time.
New way to complete your Business Identity Certificate:
For people planning on opening a new business in Lunenburg, the Town Clerk’s NEW Business Identity Certificate (BIC) is now available to be completed as part of Building Department’s Form of Intent found here: Business Identity Certificate (BIC) You will still need to print out the BIC and hand-deliver to the Town Clerk’s office, but now the form can be completed and generated online.
New Business Ribbon Cutting Ceremony:
On Thursday August 6, the Town of Lunenburg's Economic Development Committee proudly hosted its first ribbon cutting ceremony, celebrating the continued growth of Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. as the company expands into a larger office in Lunenburg. The event welcomed the business to its new space at 1 Main Street and marked the beginning of a new tradition recognizing business investment and success in our community.
Founded by Chris Kostecki, Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. has grown from a sole proprietorship into a full-service digital marketing consulting firm.
Chris was joined by members of his family, Economic Development Committee Members Joeci Gilchrest and Cathy Clark, State Representative Mike Kushmerek, State Representative Margaret Scarsdale, Beth Walsh, Constituent Services Director for State Senator John Cronin, Roy Nascimento, President & CEO of the North Central Massachusetts Chamber of Commerce, Chamber Staff and Members, Select Board members Renee Emkey, Brian Lehtinen, and Glenn McLeod, and Town Manager Jennifer Warren-Dyment.
Congratulations to Chris and the entire Diligent team on this exciting milestone. We wish you continued success and are proud that your business continues to grow right here in Lunenburg.

what_happened.line: The Appointing Committee voted unanimously to reappoint Chris Menard and Jay Simeone to full 3-year Finance Committee terms and appoint Peter Beardmore to a vacant seat.
Beardmore, a former Finance Committee and School Committee member, told the committee the town faces a long-term, not short-lived, fiscal squeeze.
The committee clarified Beardmore is filling roughly two years remaining on a term vacated by a member referred to as "Jean," not Simeone's or Menard's seat.

why_it_matters: These three now sit on the committee that reviews and recommends the town's budget before it goes to town meeting, so who holds these seats affects how budget questions get vetted.
A new member's stated view that fiscal restraint is a sustained condition, not a temporary crisis, may shape how the committee approaches future budget requests.

ours.headline: Appointing Committee reappointed Menard and Simeone and appointed Beardmore to fill a Finance Committee vacancy

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will work with the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources to learn of grant opportunities for energy conservation and renewable energy generation and will apply for appropriate grants. The Committee will ensure the Town retains its status as a designated Green Community.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will focus on improving and promoting energy efficiency in town and school facilities, infrastructure, and vehicles. The Committee will help raise awareness, educate, advise, and motivate the Town of Lunenburg residents and businesses to reduce waste, reduce energy use, conserve resources, reduce emissions/carbon footprint, and embrace clean and renewable energy options.
Responsibilities
Identify and develop grant submissions for Green Communities Competitive Grant annually that corresponds with the mission of this committee and is consistent with the Town's goals;
Develop action steps to ensure Lunenburg remains designated as a Department of Energy Resources Green Community;
Facilitate town participation in DOER programs, grants, and incentives;
Serve as an information resource for town residents and business owners on the benefits of energy and resource conservation;
Increase constituents' awareness of and promote resource conservation methods, energy efficiency programs, utility rebates, and state/federal programs to promote energy efficiency, waste reduction, recycling, and overall enhancements to long-term sustainability and resilience in response to environmental, resource, and energy challenges;
Report at least once annually on its activities to the Select Board.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of 5 regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Select Board and two associate members. Two members shall initially be appointed to a three-year term, two members shall initially be appointed to a two-year term, and one member shall initially be appointed to a one-year term. After the initial term, all regular members shall serve a three-year term. The associate members shall be appointed to a three-year term.
In addition to the regular members, the Committee shall consult with the Town Manager, the town departments that oversee the facilities and energy accounts, the School Superintendent, and the School Facilities Director that oversees the school facilities and school energy accounts in order to ascertain future energy projects, areas where energy savings are needed, and replacement schedule for vehicles.
Voting Power: All duly appointed regular members shall have full voting power.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee, the Town Manager, and the Select Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
Representations: Members shall get the approval of the Committee prior to making statements, presentations, or joining activities on behalf of the Committee.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The recording of minutes and votes of all meetings shall be conducted as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. Copies of the minutes shall be submitted to the Town Clerk as prescribed in the Town Bylaw and according to Open Meeting Law.
The Committee shall comply with all state laws and local bylaws.
This charge was adopted by the Select Board at their June 1, 2021 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting.

watch_next: Fall green-communities grant application
Fall town meeting presentation on town administration consolidation

what_happened.line: The committee missed the spring green-communities grant deadline and will apply in the fall instead.
The building design committee's direction is to renovate Turkey Hill rather than replace it, pursuing state MSBA funding.
The town is exploring consolidating town administration into one building, possibly a renovated Ritter building, with a presentation planned for fall town meeting.
Elections will move from Passios to the school building next school year, though an override vote would likely still be held at Passios.
Who owns and benefits from Turkey Hill's solar panels remains unresolved.

why_it_matters: A grant missed this spring and reapplied for in the fall affects money available for building upgrades at the schools and public safety building, not town tax rates directly.
Choosing to renovate rather than replace Turkey Hill, and pursuing MSBA funding, shapes what residents may later be asked to vote on for the school building.
Moving elections off Passios changes where most residents vote, while a possible override vote would still be held at Passios.

ours.headline: Committee missed the spring energy-grant deadline and will apply in the fall instead

watch_next: Next meeting, roughly mid-January, once PPP/National Grid building audit results are available

what_happened.line: The town met its green-communities energy-reduction goal for FY26, with buildings driving most of the drop.
A promised National Grid audit and building-by-building analysis, needed before any Turkey Hill decision, is months overdue with no date given.
Streetlight bill savings are going into the general budget with no reserve set aside for future LED maintenance.
The committee took no votes on policy; it discussed renaming itself an energy/sustainability committee and backing Tyler for an open seat.

why_it_matters: Turkey Hill and Town Hall building decisions, and any capital ask tied to them, are on hold until the overdue energy audit comes back.
Streetlight savings with no maintenance reserve means a future LED repair cost would compete with other budget lines rather than draw on savings already realized.
A committee name change and a pending appointment are procedural and do not commit the town to any spending.

ours.headline: Committee met its energy-reduction goal but remains stalled awaiting building energy audits needed for Turkey Hill decisions.

watch_next: Whether a quorum is reached at the task force's next meeting so votes can occur
Any future review of the town's ground-mount solar bylaw size cap

what_happened.line: The Green Community Task Force did not reach a quorum, so no votes or official business took place.
Members present held an informal discussion about the mini-split heat pump project at the schools, which qualified for grant funding once framed as a heat source rather than only air conditioning.
Members said they have lost access to records of what Turkey Hill's solar panels have saved since the installer went out of business.
The group discussed, without resolving, whether the town's ground-mount solar bylaw's system-size cap needs updating given improved panel efficiency.
Members described an ongoing push to get the town manager, select board, and school and town facilities to seek grant funding before bringing requests to town meeting.

why_it_matters: No quorum means nothing discussed here changed town policy or committed any funding; it was conversation, not a decision.
Whether a ground-mount solar bylaw update moves forward could affect how much of a home's electricity use residents can offset with rooftop or yard solar systems.
The task force's push to route town and school funding requests through grant review first could affect what shows up -- or doesn't -- on a future town meeting warrant.

ours.headline: No quorum was reached; members informally discussed heat pump, solar and geothermal grant projects

watch_next: A meeting with the facilities director and National Grid/Mass Save, targeted for early August, to begin the portfolio prioritization plan.
Progress on the townwide energy plan the committee plans to develop in August.

what_happened.line: The task force will seek a townwide building-assessment study through Mass Save before pursuing further building grants.
The Turkey Hill project is on hold until that assessment study is complete.
The group's main focus for August will be developing a townwide energy plan.
A resident said he will apply through the town's talent bank for appointment to the committee.

why_it_matters: The assessment study would shape which town buildings become eligible for state weatherization, heat-pump and building-management incentives, which can affect future capital budgets.
Pausing the Turkey Hill project ties its timeline to when the broader study is finished, so residents watching that project should expect delay.

A member described a past case where triggering a green grant required prevailing wage rules that raised a contractor's quote sharply -- a cost tradeoff worth watching as the town pursues more grant-funded building work.

ours.headline: Green committee will pursue a townwide Mass Save building-assessment study before its next grant push

watch_next: July 7th Green Community Task Force meeting
Tyler's expected appearance before the Select Board for associate/alternate appointment

what_happened.line: The chair pushed the school facilities director to finish two refrigeration projects and a controls upgrade that cost the town nothing, funded by Unitil incentives and the Green Grant.
Members flagged irregularities in how associate and alternate committee members are appointed and termed, and will raise wording changes with the town.
School HVAC equipment is on site and installation begins once school ends, though the state and grant funding for it does not start until July 1.
The committee tabled approval of its April 7th minutes because a member had not yet reviewed them.
The next meeting was set for July 7th, in person with a Zoom option, closing by roll-call vote.

why_it_matters: Several energy-efficiency projects at schools and town buildings are already approved and grant-funded at no cost to taxpayers, so delay in completing them is a lost-savings issue, not a budget one.
How the town appoints and terms task-force members (associate versus alternate status, five- versus seven-member structure) affects who can serve and vote on this committee going forward.
Capital-plan HVAC work at Town Hall and Ritter, and a possible library building-control system, will show up as future capital budget items residents may be asked to fund.

ours.headline: Committee pressed the schools and town to actually use already-approved, no-cost green energy grant funding.

The Historical Commission shall act for the preservation, protection, and development of the historical or archeological assets of the Town. The commission shall conduct research for places of historic or archeological value, shall seek to coordinate the activities of unofficial bodies organized for similar purposes, and may advertise, prepare, print, and distribute materials that it deems necessary for its work. It shall make recommendations to the Select Board that any place be certified as a historical landmark. The commission may hold hearings and may enter into contracts with individuals, organizations, and institutions for services furthering their objectives.
The commission may acquire in the name of the Town by gift, purchase, grant, bequest, devise, lease, or otherwise, the fee or lesser interest in real or personal property of significant historical value and may manage the same. The commission shall file an annual report which shall be included in the Annual Town Report.
The Historical Commission shall be composed of five (5) members appointed by the Select Board for terms of three years each with said terms staggered so that as nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year.

page.overview:
Lunenburg Public Library welcomes all and serves residents of the Lunenburg area as a hub for the community, enriching our lives through its collections, programs, services, facility, and people.
Please visit the Lunenburg Public Library Website for library resources, latest news, and events.
Powers and Duties - The Board of Trustees shall act as an agent of the public trust governing the library. The library shall create the general operating and administrative policies relating to budget, personnel, and contracts as specified by state law and local ordinances. All funds raised or appropriated by the town for the support and maintenance of the library shall be expended under the direction of the board. All funds that the town may receive by gift, bequest, or otherwise for library purposes shall be administered under the direction of the board in accordance with the terms of such gift, bequest, or otherwise. The board shall hire and manage the library director. The responsibilities and governance of the board shall cover the following specific areas: (i) legal; (ii) policy making; (iii) financial governance; and (iv) strategic planning. The board shall, in all matters of general municipal policy and procedure, be subject to policy directives designed to achieve uniformity and better administrative control as may from time to time be established by the town manager. The library director shall exercise professional judgment under the direction and review of the board to implement the strategic objectives and policies set by the board. The library director shall be responsible for the day-to-day administration of the library, including management of personnel, collection development, budget, physical plant, and programmatic functions, subject to policy directives established by the board. The library director shall work in conjunction with the board on strategic planning and library policies.
The Library Director shall prepare an annual budget for approval by the board. The library director shall hire library employees, fix their salaries, define their duties, make rules concerning their tenure of office and discharge them in accordance with and within the limits established by the town personnel by-laws, policies, procedures, and practices and any applicable collective bargaining agreement, in accordance with municipal policies. The board shall make all reasonable rules and regulations for the operation and management of the library system and for the conduct of its own business and affairs as may be deemed necessary. The board shall have all of the other powers and duties that are given to library trustees by general law, this charter, by-law, or other vote of the town meeting.
Composition, Term of Office - There shall be a board of trustees of the public library consisting of 7 members, elected for terms of 3 years each, so arranged that the terms of as nearly an equal number of members as is possible shall expire each year.

page.overview:
The year 2028 will mark the 300th Anniversary of the incorporation of the Town of Lunenburg. In order to recognize and celebrate Lunenburg's Tricentennial, the residents of Lunenburg, by Town Meeting vote of May 7, 2022, authorized and established a steering committee, subsequently designated the "Lunenburg 300th Anniversary Committee," and hereinafter referred to as "the Committee."
The Committee shall be comprised of no greater than 11 members, each of whom shall be appointed by the Select Board for a term to begin on the date of appointment and terminate when, as determined by a vote of the Select Board, the Committee has discharged all of its defined functions and is dissolved. As a body, the Committee shall:
Develop a celebratory plan including a timeline, proposed events, publicity plan, volunteer roster, funding requirements, and funding sources.
Coordinate with other entities and officials within the Town government, including the police chief, fire chief, DPW director, historical commission, and superintendent of schools, in order to facilitate safety and maximize resident participation.
Solicit, evaluate, and generate recommendations as to how the Town should manage the commemoration of its tricentennial, and the celebration of its rich history.
Oversee subcommittees established for specified purposes, and supervise and assist these subcommittees in their functions.
Recruit, organize, task, and oversee volunteers from among the townspeople in furtherance of the overall celebration and the execution of specific functions of the Committee and/or its subcommittees.
Plan, coordinate, manage, sponsored, and implement commemorative events including, but not limited to, recreational and educational activities and social/cultural gatherings intended to enhance the townspeople's awareness and appreciation for the history of the Town and the contributions that its residents have made locally and nationally to various fields of human endeavor including, for example, architecture, arts, civil rights, government, engineering, environmental protection, industry, invention, law, literature, medicine, the military, politics, public policy, public safety, and science.
Encourage through effective communication and outreach maximum inclusion, attendance, and participation by the townspeople in events and celebrations.
Partner with local businesses and community organizations to develop events that appeal to all ages and encourage maximum participation by town residents.

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee (formerly the TC Passios Building Design Committee) will continue to work with any contracted architectural and engineering firms, as they become available, to review space needs for town offices, school uses and community space at the building and/or land known as the TC Passios.
Additionally, the committee will work to prioritize and/or rank the existing space usage requests and explore a variety of design permutations at different estimated budget tiers that would meet the needs of the Town according to those priorities. The committee may analyze, discuss and investigate other Town-owned buildings and properties in their recommendations as they deem necessary to fulfill this charge.
This Committee will prepare viable, cost-effective solutions for the Select Board that conform to all the Town's existing financial and fiscal policies and take into consideration any/all large-scale capital expenditures projected for the next 10 years. This charge was amended by the Select Board at their January 4, 2022 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting. At the July 15, 2025 meeting of the Select Board, it was voted to add a member from the Architectural Preservation District Commission to the composition of the LMBDC and reduced the quorum to four.
