join.place: This public meeting is being conducted at the DPW office. The following informat

watch_next: November 17, 2026 special town meeting warrant article on the combined pump station contract
September 29, 2026, 6pm, Sewer Commission meeting via Zoom

what_happened.line: The commission voted to seek one combined multi-year contract for pump station operations, maintenance, emergency service and capital repair, to be recommended as a warrant article at the November 17 special town meeting.
Two privilege-fee assessments, at 786-796 Massachusetts Avenue and 67 Pratt Street, were closed out as paid and hooked up.
The commission kept its connection and privilege fee rate unchanged after hearing from town counsel.
A related operations and maintenance contract due to expire was extended to November 25 to allow more time to finish the procurement work.
The commission corrected its next meeting date from September 22 to September 29 at 6pm via Zoom.

why_it_matters: Combining pump station operations and capital repair into one multi-year contract is the mechanism voters will be asked to authorize as a warrant article at the November 17 special town meeting, shaping sewer service costs and reliability for years.
The connection and privilege fee rate staying unchanged means the cost of a new sewer hookup is not changing for now.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission voted to seek a combined multi-year pump station O&M/construction contract for Nov. town meeting

watch_next: 67 Pratt Street privilege fee assessment on a future Sewer Commission agenda
CTE operations & maintenance contract once the town manager signs it, clearing the way for a bid

what_happened.line: Town counsel recommended, and the commission accepted, continuing to charge half the betterment amount as the privilege fee on new sewer connections.
Commissioner Arthur announced his resignation over a new work schedule; the board will begin searching for a replacement once he sends a formal letter.
The two remaining sewer connections at 100 Laurel Lane were finished in-house with DPW and a masonry contractor, coming in under the original estimate.
A connection fee for condo units at 786-796 Massachusetts Ave, based on the betterment and privilege-fee formula, was presented and accepted by the property owner.
The commission will keep asking contractors to informally flag inflow/infiltration issues near connection work, without a formal betterment charge.

why_it_matters: Anyone connecting to town sewer, including at 67 Pratt Street next, will be charged under the same half-betterment privilege fee formula town counsel just reaffirmed as legally defensible.
The commission loses a member and will be recruiting a replacement, which affects who sets sewer connection and rate policy going forward.
The Laurel Lane repair closing under budget and in-house limits added cost pressure on the sewer enterprise fund, which residents' sewer fees support.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission closes out the Laurel Lane repair under budget as commissioner Arthur resigns

watch_next: Town counsel's response on whether the privilege fee must equal the original betterment
Next Sewer Commission meeting, August 25, 2026

what_happened.line: The commission found its privilege fee may be billed at half what its own bylaw requires and will ask town counsel to clarify.
Members voted to accept the first-quarter FY2027 sewer billing commitment, which includes a new rate increase.
The commission agreed to extend the current operations-and-maintenance contract into November and pursue a service-only replacement contract needing town meeting and state legislative approval.
DPW and contractor crews will begin extending sewer service near 100 Laurel Lane next week, following a resident's public-comment questions about a stub extension.

why_it_matters: If the privilege fee has been undercharged against the bylaw's stated requirement, that could change what future connecting property owners owe once town counsel weighs in.
The billing commitment sets the sewer rate charged to properties on the system this quarter, including the increase.
Replacing the O&M contract as service-only will require a town meeting vote and state legislative action before the district can act on it.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission may have billed privilege fees at half what its own bylaw requires; will recheck with town counsel

watch_next: Betterment-versus-connection-fee policy discussion on the next Sewer Commission agenda
Re-bid outcome for the 100 Laurel Lane sewer connection ahead of the November moratorium

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission rejected both bids for the stalled 100 Laurel Lane sewer connection -- one for missing paperwork, one as too high -- leaving the ADU project without a contractor.
The commission will re-bid the project before the fall digging moratorium, and a resident offered to help recruit more contractors after his family's 14-month effort on the project.
The commission opened a review of whether its decades-old betterment fees still track original construction costs, and sent the question to a future agenda.
A billing software error that misplaced a decimal point was caught manually before it overcharged a customer.

why_it_matters: A sewer connection for the Laurel Lane ADU is stalled by rejected bids and a fall digging deadline, which could push the family's project into next year.
The review of betterment fees versus a flat connection fee could change what property owners on older sewer lines pay when they connect or expand.
A billing error caught before it reached a customer's bill points to a software issue in how sewer charges are calculated.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission again rejected both 100 Laurel Lane bids, leaving the ADU project stalled before the fall moratorium

watch_next: Town council meeting next week, where the commission plans to raise its questions on connection and betterment fee wording and process
100 Laurel Lane bid opening, expected around July 21st

what_happened.line: Commission debated whether a Mass Ave two-family property was correctly charged a second residential connection fee and an additional betterment/privilege fee, and decided to raise the wording and process with town council rather than resolve it itself.
The business manager and director will keep handling individual sewer connection and betterment applications case by case, rather than bringing every one before the full commission.

A deep manhole on Prospect Street was found structurally unsound with heavy infiltration and gas levels too high for a contractor to enter, and replacement was recommended as a future project with no cost given yet.
The CTE contract's one-year term with a two-year option has run out and is going back out to bid, with an opening expected around August 3rd.
The 100 Laurel Lane project bid is out on the street, with an opening expected around July 21st and no figures yet.

why_it_matters: How the 990 Mass Ave case is resolved could set the fee owed by any Lunenburg property with more than one dwelling unit tying into the sewer, since the regulations set fees per unit and this reading has not been settled.
Keeping connection and betterment decisions with staff rather than the full commission means most property owners' fee questions get answered administratively, not in a public vote.
The Prospect Street manhole's condition points to a sewer infrastructure repair with no cost estimate yet, which would eventually show up in a future capital request.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission questioned whether a Mass Ave two-family property was correctly billed connection and betterment fees

watch_next: Draft bylaw/regulation language on a split-dwelling-unit connection fee, to be brought to the next Sewer Commission meeting
New Sewer O&M contract to go out to bid by July 8th

what_happened.line: The commission debated charging an extra sewer connection fee when a single-family home is split into more dwelling units, but made no bylaw change and directed the director to draft language for the next meeting.
Commissioners voted 5-0 to accept end-of-year billing adjustments, including a large one-time bill tied to a prolonged water leak that skewed the quarter's totals.
A specific property's betterment and connection charges were discussed as the test case for whether added living space should trigger a further connection fee.
The manhole rehabilitation contract is finished except for one manhole near Prospect Street/Laurel Lane, where unsafe gas readings mean a new bid is needed to replace it.
Commissioners voted 5-0 to keep all commission roles (chair, vice chair, clerk) unchanged.

why_it_matters: Any new connection fee for homes converted into additional dwelling units would raise costs for property owners doing that kind of renovation, once bylaw language is drafted and brought back.
The sewer operations and maintenance contract is being rebid ahead of its August expiration, which touches how sewer service is delivered without interruption.
Sewer bill delinquency and late-fee levels affect the health of the sewer enterprise fund that all ratepayers depend on.

ours.headline: Sewer board debates charging an extra connection fee when a home is split into more units

watch_next: Town counsel's opinion on whether a fee applies to single-to-multi-family sewer connection conversions
The Laurel Lane pressure-line project going out to bid once its design is finalized

what_happened.line: The commission voted to waive a resident's sewer bill after determining a water leak went into the ground rather than the sewer system.
The board decided to serve Laurel Lane properties with new pressure sewer lines instead of a gravity line, citing insufficient elevation, and will put that job out to bid.
Members could not find a bylaw provision letting the town charge an extra fee when a single-family sewer connection is converted to multi-family use, and will ask town counsel.
Completed Ashby manhole repairs close out the current contract; a new study will be needed to identify and fund the next manholes to fix.

why_it_matters: A Laurel Lane resident's sewer bill was reduced after members asked that the waived amount be stated for the record before voting, rather than approving it on a description alone.
The pressure-line project at Laurel Lane will be a bid item to watch, since it replaces an earlier plan based on a contractor estimate that turned out to be based on an installation error.
The open question on multi-family conversion fees could affect what future property owners pay when they add units, depending on what town counsel finds in the bylaw.

ours.headline: Board waived a resident's high sewer bill from a water leak and approved a pressure sewer line for Laurel Lane

watch_next: Next meeting: business manager's report on a two-family conversion fee for 990 Mass Ave
Follow-up: two additional quotes for the 100 Laurel Lane sewer tie-in

what_happened.line: The Commission rejected a single sewer tie-in estimate for 100 Laurel Lane, an amount as heard in the thousands, and ordered staff to get two more quotes.
It approved bedroom-count expansion-of-use requests at 48 West Street and 990 Mass Ave, each passing with one commissioner abstaining.
It voted to write off an uncollectible balance on a Wallace Park account after a billing error sent the wrong final-read figure to a closing attorney.
It granted a one-time bill waiver to a Leominster Road account over an unusually high usage bill, and will check in after next quarter's reading instead of granting further relief.
Staff will research whether the 990 Mass Ave two-family conversion should pay a fee beyond the standard per-bedroom charge and report back next meeting.

why_it_matters: The Laurel Lane decision means a homeowner's connection cost stays undecided while the board tests the estimate against competing bids rather than approving it outright.
The write-off and the waiver show how the sewer fund absorbs a billing mistake and a high-usage spike, costs that are ultimately spread across other ratepayers.
Whether a two-family conversion pays more than a per-bedroom fee could set the fee structure future redevelopment projects are charged under.

ours.headline: Commission balked at a $9,700 sewer tie-in bid for Laurel Lane, ordering competing quotes first

watch_next: Whether the town meets the DEP's roughly end-of-August deadline for private sewer system operation-and-maintenance plans
The drain layer's estimate for extending the line to reach 100 Laurel Lane

what_happened.line: The town faces a new, unplanned DEP requirement to document operation-and-maintenance plans for privately-owned sewer systems tied into the town system.
The commission approved the FY26 fourth-quarter sewer billing commitment by roll call vote.
Crews using old hand-drawn tie cards have not resolved sewer lateral locations at a Wallace Park-area property or at 100 Laurel Lane.
The commission is weighing a drain layer's proposal to extend an existing line at 100 Laurel Lane instead of renting a locating device.
The commission decided to keep its meeting time at 6:00 p.m. rather than reverting to an alternating 6:00/7:00 p.m. schedule.

why_it_matters: The DEP mandate could require owners of privately-owned sewer systems connected to the town system to produce plans and ordinance information on a tight timeline, and it lands on the town with no advance planning.
The approved quarterly commitment is what sets sewer billing for ratepayers this period.
Two property owners are still without a confirmed sewer lateral location, which affects their connection and any repair or extension costs.

ours.headline: Commission approved the FY26 Q4 sewer commitment and is scrambling to meet a new DEP mandate.

watch_next: Next meeting, May 12, 2026: quarter four billing commitment and town meeting feedback are scheduled agenda items.
Resolution of the 100 Laurel Lane sewer stub search remains open and undecided.

what_happened.line: The Commission previewed the sewer rate-increase slideshow it will present at town meeting, citing disposal costs and shrinking betterment revenue as drivers.
Staff said the sewer department is self-funded through user charges and would not be cut regardless of whether the town override passes.
The lowest of three or four bids was selected for the 5 Ramgren Road sewer tie-in, and work is expected to start soon.
Staff said they still cannot locate the sewer stub for 100 Laurel Lane and plan to dig to confirm whether the town owes the property a new one.
Staff confirmed the late-payment interest rate has not been raised and said the effort was to keep the minimum sewer charge low for seniors and lower-income residents.

why_it_matters: Sewer ratepayers face a rate increase that will be presented at town meeting; the size of that increase is on the slideshow the minutes describe but is not restated here.
Because the sewer fund is self-supporting through user fees, the outcome of the separate town override vote will not change sewer rates or service.
A property owner at 100 Laurel Lane may be owed a new sewer stub at town expense if the existing one cannot be located, which the commission is still investigating.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission previewed its rate-increase pitch for town meeting; says the override won't affect its budget

watch_next: The developer returning with a plan for the 14-acre lot
The chair's budget presentation at the next meeting, ahead of town meeting

what_happened.line: The commission held off deciding whether to expand the sewer district to a 14-acre lot near the driving range, pending the developer returning with an actual plan.
A commissioner said he would support letting new developments into the district only if they help fund the town's infiltration problems.
Manhole repair work was paused until nighttime temperatures rise above freezing, with follow-up needed with the contractor.
The pressure-line issue at 100 Laurel Lane remains unresolved, with the homeowner weighing a cheaper gravity connection against a costlier pump system.
The chair will prepare a budget presentation for the next meeting ahead of town meeting.

why_it_matters: Whether the sewer district expands to new land is a decision that could eventually reach a town meeting warrant article, and the commission has tied any expansion to whether new development helps pay for the town's existing infiltration problems.
The commission's budget will be presented at an upcoming meeting ahead of town meeting, which is where residents get a vote on it.
A private connection dispute at 100 Laurel Lane affects what one homeowner pays to hook into town sewer, and the underlying pressure-line question is still open.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission holds off deciding on expanding the district to a 14-acre lot near the driving range

watch_next: Town meeting vote on the FY27 sewer budget and rate increase
Pawn Street property owner's decision on funding engineering plans for a sewer district connection

what_happened.line: A commissioner found a discontinued pump line pouring groundwater into the sewer system on Laurel Lane, and the leak will be added to the contractor's sealing work.
The FY27 sewer budget and a rate increase, already approved at a prior meeting, moves forward to a town meeting vote.
The board said funds are too tight at fiscal year end to widen the search for other infiltration hot spots flagged in past studies.
The commission discussed a policy requiring developers who add sewer capacity to offset it by fixing an equivalent amount of leaking pipe elsewhere in town.
A resident's request to connect a Pawn Street property to the sewer district stays on hold pending the owner's decision on funding engineering plans.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on the FY27 sewer budget and rate increase at town meeting, which sets what sewer bills look like next year.
Groundwater leaking into the system through manholes and old pump lines adds to what the sewer system has to carry and treat, which is part of what any future rate increase would be paying to fix.
A developer offset requirement, if adopted, would shift some of the cost of fixing leaking infrastructure onto new development rather than existing ratepayers.

ours.headline: Sewer board finds major manhole water infiltration on Laurel Lane but can't fund a wider search this year

watch_next: Sewer Commission meeting, March 31, 2026 (developer's extension plan and possible commission support)
Annual Town Meeting, May 2, 2026 (sewer extension petition, bylaw amendment, and storm water utility articles)

what_happened.line: The Commission recommended the developer file a citizen's petition warrant article by March 16 to extend sewer service up Pond Street for a proposed duplex subdivision.
The developer was asked to return March 31 so the Commission could consider giving its "blessing" to the extension plan before town meeting.
A sewer bylaw wording change tied to the new ADU bylaw, already reviewed by town counsel, is headed to town meeting for a vote.
The FY27 sewer rate proposal shifts more of the increase onto higher water users, and this year's budget avoids drawing on retained earnings.
A separate storm water utility fee, which would bill residents apart from the sewer bill, is also headed to a town meeting warrant article.

why_it_matters: Extending sewer service to a new subdivision is a decision residents will see as a warrant article at the May 2 town meeting.
The FY27 rate structure and bylaw changes affect what appears on sewer bills and how future accessory dwelling units connect to the system.
A new storm water utility fee would be a separate charge on top of the existing sewer bill if adopted at town meeting.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission weighed extending sewer service for a proposed duplex development via town meeting warrant article

watch_next: March 10 Sewer Commission meeting: review and possible finalization of the draft sewer-connection policy
May town meeting: storm water utility ballot question

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to approve its FY27 enterprise budget, raising the minimum charge and regular user rate to close a revenue gap.
The commission said declining betterment payments, as 20-year financing plans from the system's original construction wind down, are driving the gap.
Commissioners moved to schedule a joint meeting with the Select Board to consider appointing a fifth commissioner.
A proposed town-wide storm water utility, billing based on impervious surface for most properties, was discussed ahead of a May town meeting ballot question.
A draft sewer-connection policy was tabled, with review and possible finalization set for the March 10 meeting to meet the town meeting warrant deadline.

why_it_matters: Sewer customers will see higher minimum and usage charges on their bills as the self-funded sewer enterprise fund raises rates to replace declining betterment revenue.
Residents will be asked to vote on a separate storm water utility fee at May town meeting, in addition to their sewer and property tax bills.
The sewer-connection policy under review could set new terms for future hookups before the next town meeting warrant closes.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission voted to approve its FY27 budget, which raises user rates to close a revenue gap.

watch_next: February 24, 2026 Sewer Commission meeting (Zoom, 6 p.m.) -- public comment invited on the FY27 rate increase
A vote on the finalized FY27 rate structure once budget figures are set

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission postponed a vote on a proposed FY27 rate increase, waiting for finalized budget figures from the new finance director.
The proposed increase is meant to pass through rising disposal costs charged by Fitchburg and Leominster and cover falling betterment income.
Commissioners leaned toward holding the minimum sewer charge lower and shifting more of any increase onto higher-usage customers.
The commission approved the FY25 annual report, which showed retained earnings were used to balance the sewer budget, a practice it wants to reduce.
The commission voted to move its in-person meetings to 6 p.m. and will take public comment on the rate increase at its next meeting.

why_it_matters: Sewer customers will see a rate increase on a future bill, and how the minimum charge is set will determine how much low-usage households pay versus heavy users.
Using retained earnings to balance the sewer budget defers costs rather than resolving them, which can point toward a larger rate increase later.
Residents will get a chance to comment on the proposed rate before the commission takes a final vote.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission tables a proposed FY27 rate hike (around 16%) pending finalized budget numbers

watch_next: Spring special town meeting warrant for the sewer tie-in and ADU regulation articles
Next Sewer Commission meeting agenda, where the tie-in proposal is to be formally taken up

what_happened.line: The Commission will bring a proposed rule to the spring special town meeting requiring new sewer hookups to tie into the line on the street the property is actually addressed to.
That regulation will be prepped alongside pending ADU (accessory dwelling unit) rule changes, both headed to town counsel before the meeting.
The tie-in rule follows a recent dispute over a Chestnut Street sewer connection.
The business manager reported a large share of this quarter's sewer bills still unpaid, with unpaid FY25 balances going onto property tax liens.
No votes were taken beyond approving prior minutes and adjourning.

why_it_matters: A new sewer-connection rule tying hookups to a property's addressed street would affect anyone building or connecting near a lot line where two streets have sewer mains, and it goes to a town meeting vote in the spring.
Unpaid sewer bills that convert to tax liens attach to the property, not just the account, so residents behind on sewer charges could see that debt show up on their tax bill.
ADU regulation and easement language, still pending town counsel review, will shape what accessory dwelling units are allowed to do about sewer access.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission moved to require new hookups tie into the line on their own addressed street

watch_next: A future Sewer Commission agenda item drafting the street-tie-in-only regulation
Next meeting: December 9 at 7pm (hybrid)

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted down a sewer easement waiver for the 763 Massachusetts Ave duplex conversion project.
All members present voted against the waiver, denying the developer's request to use an easement instead of a direct street tie-in.
The commission adopted a new one-time connection charge policy for accessory dwelling units, based on Title 5 flow.
Members agreed to draft a future regulation requiring sewer connections to run to a property's own street rather than through an easement.
The commission granted the manhole-replacement contractor an extension to June 30, 2026, since roads cannot be reopened after mid-November.

why_it_matters: The denied waiver means the 763 Massachusetts Ave duplex project cannot proceed with an easement-based sewer connection and would need a different, likely costlier, tie-in approach.
A future regulation requiring direct street tie-ins instead of easements could affect how other properties near shared sewer mains are allowed to connect going forward.
Owners adding accessory dwelling units will now face a one-time sewer connection charge calculated per gallon under Title 5 flow standards.

ours.headline: Commission voted down a sewer easement waiver for the 763 Massachusetts Ave duplex project

watch_next: Next Sewer Commission meeting, November 25 (in person): continuation of the 763 Massachusetts Ave hearing with stub location, pipe size, and Chestnut Street cost comparison
May town meeting: proposed bylaw wording change from "emergency" to "unusual and extraordinary"

what_happened.line: Commission continued the 763 Massachusetts Ave easement waiver so the applicant can locate an existing sewer stub and pin down pipe size.

Members debated whether granting that waiver would foreclose ever extending sewer service down Chestnut Street, and asked for a cost comparison of a Chestnut Street main versus three separate tie-ins.
A separate, smaller easement waiver for 830/832 Massachusetts Ave was voted and passed.
Town counsel recommended replacing "emergency" with "unusual and extraordinary" in the waiver bylaw wording, with the change headed to May town meeting.
A manhole frame/grate repair project is delayed because the replacement frames arrived the wrong size.

why_it_matters: A decision on the 763 Massachusetts Ave request could shape whether Chestnut Street ever gets sewer service, and who pays for it, so its continuation keeps that choice open for now.
The wording change to the waiver bylaw is headed to a town meeting vote in May, which residents will be asked to approve.
Property owners facing sewer tie-in costs should watch how the commission resolves the betterment-charge question raised in this hearing.

ours.headline: Commission tabled a 763 Mass Ave sewer easement to weigh extending service down Chestnut Street

watch_next: October 28th Sewer Commission meeting: continuance of the 830/832 Massachusetts Ave hearing and a vote on the capital reserve warrant article

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission granted a sewer easement waiver for 792 Massachusetts Avenue (Stone Farm) on a 3-0 vote.
A hearing on an easement waiver for 830/832 Massachusetts Avenue could not proceed for lack of a voting quorum, after one member recused and another was absent.
That hearing was formally continued to the October 28th meeting on a 3-0 vote.
A decision on whether to add a capital reserve line item to the November Town Meeting warrant was pushed to the October 28th meeting instead of being taken up tonight.
A related waiver request for 763 Massachusetts Avenue (the old funeral home) was not voted on because it was not properly listed on tonight's agenda.

why_it_matters: The 792 Massachusetts Avenue waiver clears a sewer easement step for that property, while owners at 830/832 and 763 Massachusetts Avenue still have unresolved hearings pending action on October 28th.
Whether a capital reserve line goes on the November Town Meeting warrant is a question residents may be asked to vote on directly.
The commission has a vacant seat and asked residents interested in serving to contact the DPW office or Town Hall.

ours.headline: Granted an easement waiver for a Massachusetts Ave sewer project; continued another hearing for lack of quorum

watch_next: October 14 Sewer Commission meeting, including the easement waiver hearing for 830/832 Massachusetts Ave
Town counsel review of the ADU sewer regulations, expected ahead of a town meeting vote

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission approved a flow-increase for a new fitness facility at 308 Massachusetts Ave, replacing a lower-use tenant.
Commissioners kept working on connection fees and regulations for accessory dwelling units, still short of a final vote.
The ADU rules still need town counsel review, then a town meeting vote, likely at the November annual meeting.
A commissioner will step out of part of the October 14 meeting covering an easement waiver at a property he is personally involved with.

why_it_matters: The flow-increase vote is what lets a business change, like a new gym, connect to town sewer at its actual level of use.
The ADU connection fee, once it clears town counsel and a town meeting vote, would set what a homeowner pays to add sewer service for an accessory dwelling.
The recusal keeps a commissioner from voting on a matter involving his own property, a routine conflict-of-interest step ahead of that hearing.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission approved a flow-increase for a new Massachusetts Ave gym and advanced ADU connection fees

watch_next: Next Sewer Commission meeting: consolidated ADU fee draft for discussion before it goes to town council
Future meeting: flow-increase vote on the retail-to-gym change of use and two easement waiver requests

what_happened.line: Commission drafted ADU sewer connection fees and tie-in rules but took no final vote, planning one consolidated draft before town council.
Commission voted to credit a resident's sewer bill after a water-meter change had inflated her usage reading.
Draft rule discussed: an ADU line must tie into the existing house line, not connect directly to the street, or pay a full new-connection fee.
Commission previewed two upcoming easement waiver requests and a flow-increase vote for a retail space becoming a gym.

why_it_matters: Anyone adding an accessory dwelling unit will owe a sewer connection fee that is still being drafted, not yet set or voted.
A water-meter change can move a sewer bill on its own, as this credit shows, without any error by the resident.
The change-of-use flow vote and easement waivers ahead touch how much sewer capacity other properties can claim.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission drafted proposed ADU sewer connection fees and tie-in rules but took no final vote on them.

watch_next: The draft ADU sewer regulation, once commissioners' notes are compiled by staff
The public hearing that must precede any vote to adopt the regulation

what_happened.line: Sewer Commission agreed to draft its own regulation covering ADU sewer tie-ins, fees, easements, and septic-to-sewer conversions, after a morning meeting with town counsel.
Each commissioner agreed to write individual notes and ideas for the ADU regulation and send them to staff, rather than one person drafting alone.
The commission voted to approve a billing correction for a resident at 17 Renny Street after a water-meter mix-up between two addresses.
Commissioners agreed to compare notes with Leominster and Fitchburg on any ADU sewer fees or regulations those towns have adopted.
The commission set its adoption process: draft the regulation internally, send it to town counsel for review, then hold a public hearing before voting it in.

why_it_matters: Any resident adding an accessory dwelling unit will eventually face whatever tie-in fees, meter rules, and septic-conversion requirements this regulation sets, once it goes through a public hearing.
A billing correction for one water/sewer account was approved, a reminder that meter records can be checked and fixed when a mix-up is found.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission began drafting new sewer regulations for accessory dwelling units after meeting with town counsel

watch_next: A noticed public hearing on the Sunny Hill Drive easement, once the developer's presentation is ready
August 21 Town Council meeting on the ADU sewer connection bylaw

what_happened.line: A developer asked the Sewer Commission for an easement across town land to serve a new Sunny Hill Drive subdivision; no decision was made.
The commission asked the developer to prepare a full presentation before bringing the easement to a formal public hearing.
Any formal easement request will need a noticed public hearing with at least five days' newspaper notice.
The commission voted to accept the FY2026 sewer billing commitment.
A billing-vendor software upgrade delayed the first-quarter FY26 bill run and caused old 2023 bills to reprint.

why_it_matters: The easement request touches how much say the town keeps over private development on town-owned land, and how future accessory dwelling units connect to sewer -- residents will get a formal hearing before anything is decided.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission weighed letting a developer easement across town land for a new subdivision, decided nothing yet

watch_next: August 21 meeting with town counsel on ADU fee and easement regulations
Next regular Sewer Commission meeting, August 12, 2025

what_happened.line: The commission left a proposed flat fee for ADU sewer connections undecided, with no vote taken.
It referred a new NPDES permit's annual system-mapping requirement to engineering firm Wright-Pierce rather than setting a cost or schedule.
Only one or two commissioners plan to attend an August 21 meeting with town counsel on ADU and easement rules, to avoid triggering public-meeting quorum.
Commissioner Bill Bernard will recuse himself from a Massachusetts Avenue easement dispute because he was contracted for the original sewer install there.
The Dana Street pump station repair, completed with FY25 funds before the fiscal year closed, is being dropped from future agendas.

why_it_matters: A flat ADU sewer-connection fee, once set, would become a new cost for any homeowner adding an accessory dwelling unit tied into town sewer.
The NPDES mapping mandate could raise sewer department costs, and sewer department costs are typically recovered through sewer fees rather than the tax levy.
How the commission staffs its August 21 meeting and who recuses on the Massachusetts Ave easement case shapes how openly those decisions get made.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission weighed a flat ADU inspection fee and costly new NPDES mapping rules; no votes taken on either.

watch_next: The commission's draft letter to the town board proposing an ADU fee structure, after checking with legal
Future meeting agendas where the ADU fee question remains open for further research

what_happened.line: The commission decided to draft a letter to the town board raising a new hookup/bedroom fee for accessory dwelling units, without setting a fee amount.
Commissioners voted to accept FY25 year-end billing adjustments, with the amount as heard varying between readings in the recording.
A commissioner questioned why the engineering contract requires full system mapping every year rather than less often, and asked staff to check whether that is required by statute.
The business manager said the sewer delinquency rate appears lower than previously stated, though it is too early to assess the new fiscal year's collections.

why_it_matters: A new ADU hookup or per-bedroom sewer fee would affect anyone adding an accessory dwelling unit or extra bedroom, though no rate has been proposed yet.
The FY25 adjustment vote and delinquency discussion touch how sewer bills are calculated and collected, which flows into the rates the district charges.
The question about the engineering contract's annual mapping requirement could affect what the sewer system spends on outside engineering services, a cost eventually built into rates.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission weighs creating new hookup/bedroom fees for accessory dwelling units.

watch_next: Research from other towns (e.g., Fitchburg, Leominster) on ADU sewer fees, to be brought back to the commission
Next meetings: July 8, July 29, August 12, August 26

what_happened.line: Commission discussed charging accessory dwelling units a sewer hookup fee, tentatively favoring half the standard fee, but set no fee.
A Munis billing update had added an incorrect late fee to overdue quarterly sewer demands; the business manager reversed the erroneous charges before bills go out.
Dana Street pump station bypass repair work is tentatively scheduled to begin June 30.
Manhole repair work is tentatively scheduled to begin in July, pending a compliance review.
About 48 boxes of old files dating to 1994 are being disposed of, with the state notified; no commission vote was needed.

why_it_matters: Any accessory-dwelling-unit sewer fee the commission eventually adopts would be a new charge on property owners adding such units, and none has been set yet.
A billing-system error that misapplied late fees on quarterly sewer demands was caught and corrected before bills went out, so no ratepayer should see the wrong charge on this cycle's demand.
The pump station and manhole repairs are maintenance work on existing sewer infrastructure, not new costs described in this meeting.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission opened discussion on charging a fee for accessory dwelling unit (ADU) sewer hookups, with no fee set yet

watch_next: A future Sewer Commission meeting where staff bring back research on an ADU/accessory-unit connection fee

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission put off deciding a new sewer hookup fee for accessory dwelling units, sending it to staff for research.
New state rules that ease building in-law apartments left the existing connection-fee policy unclear on how to charge them.
The commission approved a scope of engineering work with its longtime firm covering permitting, system mapping and planning, without seeking competing bids.
Staff said homeowners with aging septic systems have been calling to ask what a sewer hookup would cost them.
The commission agreed to resume recruiting a new member after one member said he is leaving.

why_it_matters: Anyone building or converting a space into an accessory dwelling unit will be affected by whatever hookup fee the commission eventually sets.
Homeowners near the sewer line, especially those with failing septic systems, have a direct stake in how connection costs are structured.
The engineering contract and the commission's own membership affect who plans and executes the town's sewer infrastructure work going forward.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission debated charging a new hookup fee for accessory dwelling units, deferring it to next meeting

watch_next: Next meeting, June 10, 2025: update on Dana Street repair and warranty inquiry, plus manhole repair contract progress.

what_happened.line: Commission voted to proceed with an emergency force main repair at the Dana Street pump station.
Commission reorganized, electing Brett Ramston chair, Scott Dah vice chair, and Dan Proctor clerk.
A Munis billing error reverted sewer rates to an old schedule during a bill run, requiring supplemental Q4 billing to correct affected accounts.
A manhole repair contract was awarded to Insituform Technologies, funded partly by ARPA/OPA money with the remainder from the commission's budget.

why_it_matters: The Dana Street repair draws on a capital line item the commission says was set aside for this work, and staff were asked to check for a warranty without delaying the approved repair.
Sewer customers whose Q4 bill was set under the reverted rate schedule should expect a supplemental bill correcting it to the current rate.
The manhole repair contract, tied to a federal ARPA/OPA grant with town funds covering the balance, addresses infiltration and inflow into the sewer system.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission elected new officers and approved emergency Dana Street pump station repair work.

watch_next: Next meeting, May 27 (Zoom, 6pm), where the billing review ahead of FY26 and new-hire start are on the agenda
Dana Street sewer work update, added to the next meeting's agenda

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to accept a regular and a supplemental billing commitment after a billing-system error reverted many quarterly bills to outdated 2022 rates.
A customer's unusually low bill first tipped off staff that accounts above the minimum charge were being billed at the wrong rate.
Corrective bills are going out to recover the underbilled revenue, with most per-account differences described as modest.
The commission agreed, without a formal vote, to send a revised recruitment letter for its vacant elected seat, reusing the prior water-customer mailing list.
A new business-office assistant starts May 27, and manhole-repair work is expected to begin in June.

why_it_matters: Customers billed above the minimum charge may receive a corrected bill reflecting current rates rather than the stale 2022 rate the system applied.
The sewer fund's revenue depends on those corrective bills going out and being paid, since the reverted rates undercharged a large share of accounts for a period.
The commission's elected seat stays vacant, leaving one fewer voice on rate and budget decisions until someone is recruited.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission found ~500 quarterly bills used stale 2022 rates, is sending corrective bills to recover ~$24,000

watch_next: Town meeting vote on warrant articles 21-24 (OPEB transfer, sewer budget, I&I fund, reserve capacity fund)
Next commission meeting for a draft recruitment letter addressing commission vacancies

what_happened.line: The FY26 sewer budget going to town meeting is balanced with retained earnings and carries no rate increase this year.
The director told the commission that rising costs mean sewer rates will likely need to increase next year.
Warrant articles moving money into the OPEB, inflow-and-infiltration, and reserve capacity funds are slated for the town meeting consent calendar as non-controversial.
A Munis billing error was caught and corrected during fourth-quarter reconciliation, and a resident's concern about uncollected sewer billing was raised again.
The commission recommended a candidate for hire as assistant to the business manager, with a start date expected in late May.

why_it_matters: No sewer rate hike is proposed this year, but the director's warning means residents should expect one to come up for a vote next budget cycle.
The sewer budget and three fund-transfer articles go before town meeting, where they are expected to pass without debate on the consent calendar.
Recurring software errors and unresolved uncollected billing touch the accuracy of individual sewer bills, separate from the budget vote itself.

ours.headline: Sewer budget for town meeting draws on retained earnings; no rate hike now, but one is expected next year

watch_next: The future meeting where sewer enterprise capital improvement line items are rearranged and voted on
Resolution of Commissioner Hurley's appointment term given his planned move

what_happened.line: Commission voted to reimburse the town from the sewer enterprise fund for the DPW director's time covering the vacant business manager role.
Line items will be rearranged at a future meeting to fund that reimbursement from the capital improvement account, not as a formal transfer.
Commissioners also voted to waive interest and accept final payment on a sold property's sewer account.
A partial-payment option was approved for the online sewer and water billing system, letting customers behind on a bill pay something.

why_it_matters: The reimbursement moves a cost tied to a town staffing vacancy onto the sewer enterprise fund, which sewer and water ratepayers support.
The new partial-payment option changes how customers behind on a sewer or water bill can settle what they owe, rather than being blocked from paying at all.
The capital improvement account line-item rearrangement is a budget change residents should look for when it comes back for a formal vote.

ours.headline: Sewer Commission voted to reimburse the town over $14,000 for the DPW director covering the business manager vacancy

page.overview:
The Sewer Commission office is in the DPW Building at 520 Chase Road - the office is open from 7 am to 3 pm. The Commission regularly meets twice a month. The Commission meetings historically were held on the 2nd Tuesday (at the DPW Building) and the last Tuesday (in person at Town Hall) but check each posted agenda to be sure.
The Commission has been holding its meetings via Zoom. The links to the Zoom meetings are found with the posted agendas for public participation. Then the meeting recordings are found on the Lunenburg Access channel/YouTube.
The Sewer Commission is a five-member elected board. The Sewer Commission works in concert with the DPW and DPW Director to plan and implement changes, upgrades, and maintenance. Note: the Town's public water supply is administered by the Lunenburg Water District 978-582-4532 and is a separate entity from the Town. If you need a Betterment Payoff amount or Release of Lien, please Email Tax Collectors' Office or call 978-582-4132.
The Charter
The Sewer Commissioners shall make careful studies of the resources, possibilities, and needs of the Town as they relate to the availability of sanitary sewers and shall make plans for the installation of a system of sanitary sewers and for the maintenance of a sanitary sewer system. The Sewer Commission shall develop a comprehensive or master plan for a town-wide system of sanitary sewers, setting forth, in graphic and textual form, policies to govern the future growth and development of the entire Town. The Board of Sewer Commissioners shall, in conjunction with other land use bodies, assist in developing a long-range strategic plan for guiding town growth and development. The powers and authority of the Sewer Commission shall include oversight of the Sewer Enterprise Fund, setting rates and charges for the use of the sanitary sewer system, ratification responsibility for the Sewer Business Manager, and providing advice to the Board of Selectmen relating to intergovernmental agreements concerning sanitary sewers. The day-to-day operation, care, and maintenance of the sanitary sewers shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager. The Sewer Commission shall make an annual report to the Town Meeting, including a full accounting of the Sewer Enterprise Fund, information regarding the condition of the Town's sewer system and any plans or proposals for its development, and estimates of their cost.

what_happened.line: The task force voted unanimously by roll call to accept its stormwater warrant article, with town counsel's edits, for the special town meeting.
The approved article is to go out that night to town staff for filing ahead of the meeting.
Members are working to schedule presentations to FinCom, the Select Board, and a public information session before the November 17 town meeting.
The next task force meeting, September 21, will finalize what those presentations say about the budget and the funding-mechanism options.

why_it_matters: This sends a stormwater program to a warrant article residents will vote on at the November 17 special town meeting.
How the program is funded -- a utility-style fee versus a blended approach -- changes how costs split between the town, commercial and industrial properties, which can show up as a bill.
FinCom and Select Board presentations, still being scheduled, are where that funding-mechanism choice gets debated before the vote.

ours.headline: Task force approved its stormwater warrant article for special town meeting by unanimous roll call.

watch_next: Warrant article language due September 17, after task force votes on it around September 8 and 14
November 17 special town meeting: non-binding straw poll on utility vs. operating-budget funding

what_happened.line: The task force will ask a non-binding straw poll of town meeting to choose between a stormwater utility fee and continuing to fund stormwater work through the operating budget.
Members settled on billing every property a flat fee based on its impervious surface (an ERU approach) rather than tiered rates, if a utility is chosen.
Fees would be billed separately from the property tax bill, payable quarterly by tear-off coupon; municipal land would not be billed but churches and nonprofits would be.
A warrant article is due September 17, with two task force meetings around September 8 and 14 to draft and vote on its language before sending it to town counsel.
FinCom hears the proposal October 8, the Select Board October 20, and a public information session is planned around November 3, ahead of the November 17 special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Depending on which funding path town meeting favors in the non-binding vote, residents could see stormwater costs shift from the tax bill to a new separate utility bill tied to a property's paved and roofed area.
Churches, nonprofits and large commercial parcels would be billed under a utility approach even though they are often exempt from property tax, while town-owned land would not be billed.
The vote at town meeting is advisory only; the operating-budget alternative includes a stormwater engineer position that failed as an override once already.

ours.headline: Task force will draft a non-binding article asking town meeting to choose stormwater utility vs. operating budget funding

watch_next: Non-binding straw poll at fall town meeting on utility fee vs. tax funding
Possible short Zoom meeting August 31 to meet the warrant deadline

what_happened.line: Task force will seek a non-binding straw poll at fall town meeting on utility fee vs. tax funding, not a bylaw vote.
Members drafted a phased abatement/credit schedule for a future stormwater utility fee.
GIS and assessor staff will re-inspect and correct impervious-area data for several properties.
Group plans to invite the finance official next meeting and may hold a short Zoom session in late August to meet the town meeting warrant deadline.

why_it_matters: This affects how stormwater infrastructure work gets paid for going forward -- through a new dedicated utility bill or through the existing property tax/operating budget.
The fall town meeting question is a straw poll to gauge preference, not a binding vote, so no funding change would take effect from it alone.
A future utility fee would include an abatement/credit option for properties, which could affect what an individual property owner eventually owes.

ours.headline: Task force to seek a non-binding straw poll at fall town meeting on stormwater utility vs. tax funding

watch_next: Stormwater Task Force meeting, July 13, 2026
Stormwater Task Force meeting, July 30, 2026

what_happened.line: The task force leaned toward funding stormwater work through a stand-alone utility fee rather than the operating budget.
Members spent most of the meeting correcting property-by-property use codes and impervious-area data feeding the fee model.
The task force set billing rules combining fees for storage bays, apartments and adjoining lots, while keeping some condos billed per unit.
Combining the sewer and a new stormwater commission would need state legislative action, so it is not being pursued now.
Next task force meetings are set for July 13 and July 30, with a bylaw draft due before a possible fall Town Meeting article.

why_it_matters: Whether stormwater costs land on the tax bill or a separate utility fee changes how much residential versus commercial property owners pay.
The property-by-property review, including exceptions for condos, storage units and mixed-ownership sites, will determine each parcel's individual fee.
A fall Town Meeting article would ask voters to act on the funding mechanism and any bylaw the task force drafts.

ours.headline: Task force keeps refining property-by-property stormwater fee data and leans toward a utility, not the operating budget

watch_next: Next task force meeting, tentatively June 24 (fallback June 29)
Fall special town meeting vote on operating-budget vs. stand-alone utility funding for stormwater fees

what_happened.line: The task force decided to bill the Carousel Lane/Emerald Place condo complex as one combined property rather than unit by unit.
The Lunenburg Housing Authority's White Street property was flagged as a likely exception, since billing it would mean the town taxing itself.

Members discussed presenting voters two funding options at the fall special town meeting: folding the fee into the operating budget, where it would rise with the annual levy, or a stand-alone utility fee.
Working consensus was reached on ERU assignments for several property categories, including accessory lots and multi-unit parcels billed on one tax bill.
No formal vote was taken on the methodology; members got homework to review the ERU list before the next meeting, tentatively June 24.

why_it_matters: Every property in town, including condos, duplexes and multi-house lots, is being assigned a stormwater fee based on impervious surface, which will eventually appear on a bill.
Voters will be asked at the fall special town meeting to choose how the stormwater program is funded, a choice that affects whether the fee rises automatically with the town's annual tax levy.
Owners of shared or multi-unit properties should watch how their property is classified, since billing decisions are being made property-by-property rather than unit-by-unit.

ours.headline: Task force is assigning stormwater ERU fees property-by-property, leaning toward per-ERU billing over flat tiers

watch_next: Next meeting: May 14
The side-by-side operating-budget vs. utility cost comparison for the next public/Finance Committee presentation

what_happened.line: No decision was made on funding stormwater through a new utility fee versus the town's tax-funded operating budget, after debate over utility overhead.
The group agreed to build a comparison of operating-budget cost, utility cost, and the difference between them for a future presentation.
That presentation will focus on the financial impact and cost comparison to residents, not general stormwater education.
A property-fee model is being built from GIS impervious-surface data for roughly 700 properties, with a fee to be calculated for each.
The next meeting is set for May 14.

why_it_matters: This decides whether stormwater work shows up as a new separate fee on a resident's bill or stays folded into the property tax rate.
How overhead and cost are split between a stand-alone utility and the operating budget could shift how much of the cost businesses versus homeowners pay.
No funding method has been chosen yet; the task force is still building the cost comparison that would inform that choice.

ours.headline: Task force debated funding storm water via a new utility fee vs. a tax override, sparring over overhead

watch_next: Next Stormwater Task Force meeting, tentatively April 16
Town's Proposition 2.5 override vote, which now carries the stormwater compliance funding question

what_happened.line: Task force voted 5-0 to pull the stormwater utility bylaw from the May town meeting warrant.
Members agreed the bylaw would compete for attention with the town's pending override votes and that public education on it had been too limited.
No consensus formed to put a separate override article on the warrant to fully fund MS4 stormwater compliance instead.
A resident pressed the task force on whether a future utility fee would split fairly between commercial and residential properties, citing the town's single tax rate policy.
The task force agreed to look further into the commercial/residential split with the assessor's office and local business owners before any future utility push.

why_it_matters: The stormwater utility bylaw, which would have created a separate fee to fund MS4 permit compliance, will not appear on the May town meeting warrant this year.

MS4 stormwater compliance funding was reduced in the town manager's override budget proposal at a recent select board workshop, leaving the item bundled into the override question rather than funded separately.

Any future stormwater utility proposal would set fees by property type, including commercial properties, and the task force has committed to studying that split with the assessor's office before proceeding.

ours.headline: Task force voted to pull the stormwater utility bylaw from the May town meeting warrant, deferring to the override vote

watch_next: Spring town meeting: vote on the stormwater utility enabling legislation and bylaw
Fall town meeting: vote on the stormwater budget that determines when fee collection begins

what_happened.line: Task force will bring stormwater utility enabling legislation and a bylaw to spring town meeting for a vote.
Fee collection would not start until after fall town meeting separately approves the stormwater budget.
Proposed fees would be based on a property's impervious surface area rather than its assessed value.
Residents asked whether state-maintained roads, tax-exempt and agricultural properties would pay the fee, and why a credit for on-site stormwater management is capped rather than full.
No fee, budget, or bylaw vote was taken at this meeting; it was presentation and discussion only.

why_it_matters: A vote at spring town meeting would create a new stormwater fee, billed by impervious surface area, separate from the property tax bill.
A second vote at fall town meeting would set the budget the fee actually funds, so residents get two separate decisions before any bill arrives.
Owners of large paved lots -- commercial, some agricultural -- would likely see a larger fee than most homes, where a capped flat fee is proposed.

ours.headline: Task force outlined a proposed stormwater utility fee; bylaw goes to spring town meeting, fees start later.

watch_next: The public presentation at the library, once room/screen logistics are confirmed
Jarice's finalized slide deck, due the day after this meeting

what_happened.line: The task force decided the fee structure stays under select board oversight rather than pursuing a separate sewer/storm commission, which would need a multi-year legislative process.
Members kept a 50% cap on stormwater credits and abatements in the public presentation, matching what other Massachusetts communities with similar utilities offer.
A caveat will be added noting the proposed fee is not guaranteed to stay flat, given uncertainty from a pending new EPA stormwater permit.
A funding-use slide line item for drainage improvement projects was removed because that work is not currently budgeted through the utility.
No fee amount was set; the meeting was spent revising slides and an FAQ ahead of an upcoming public presentation, with a final deck due from Jarice the next day.

why_it_matters: This is preparation for a proposed town-wide stormwater fee that would appear on future water/sewer or tax bills; no rate has been adopted yet.
Keeping fee governance with the select board, rather than creating a new sewer/storm commission, means the same elected board residents already interact with would continue to set this fee.
A 50% cap on credits limits how much a property owner could reduce the fee through stormwater management practices, and the fee amount itself is described as unstable pending a new EPA permit.

ours.headline: Task force fine-tuned its draft public presentation on a proposed town-wide stormwater utility fee; no fee was set.

watch_next: March 5, 7:15-8:30 PM: public information session on the stormwater bylaw
February 24 task force meeting: finalizing bylaw language ahead of the public hearing

what_happened.line: The task force will ask the sewer commission to take on stormwater billing and possibly serve as the stormwater commission, to avoid hiring a dedicated engineer or admin.
The bylaw draft was corrected so the stormwater commission, not the select board, approves future fee changes.
A public information session on the stormwater bylaw is set for 7:15-8:30 PM Thursday, March 5th, the only such session before town meeting.

Members ran sample fee calculations for commercial properties and compared funding the work through the town budget versus a utility fee, without settling on either approach or on hiring in-house staff.
The next task force meeting is set for Tuesday, February 24th, to finalize the bylaw before a public hearing.

why_it_matters: The stormwater bylaw is the only article going to this town meeting, so how it funds fee billing and inspections -- through the sewer department or new staff -- will shape what residents and businesses are asked to pay.
Whether the fee is structured as a utility charge or folded into a Prop 2½ override changes who approves future rate increases and how it shows up on a resident's tax bill.
The March 5th session is the only public briefing before the vote, so residents wanting to weigh in on the bylaw or its fee structure have one scheduled chance to do so.

ours.headline: Task force preps stormwater fee bylaw and March 5 info session; still undecided on override size, engineer hire

watch_next: Select Board bylaw and governance discussion, February 10
May annual town meeting: storm water utility bylaw vote

what_happened.line: The task force agreed to split town meeting action in two: bring the storm water bylaw to the May annual town meeting first, and hold the fee and rate structure for a later special town meeting.
The draft bylaw and governance options -- a five-member elected board, a three-member elected board, or an appointed commission -- go to the Select Board ahead of its February 10 session.
The board set a run of dates: Finance Committee on February 5, Select Board on February 10, a public information session March 5, and the task force's own next meeting February 19.
The group leaned toward moving billing from quarterly to annual and looking at piggybacking it on the tax or sewer bill to cut postage costs.
No formal vote was taken on the budget or fee numbers; members debated at length how much fee detail to show the Finance Committee, without resolving it.

why_it_matters: This is the early groundwork for a new stormwater utility fee that would eventually appear as its own charge on property owners, separate from the tax rate itself.
Splitting the bylaw vote from the fee vote means the May town meeting decision on structure and governance would come before residents see a final rate or fee schedule.
How the bill is delivered -- annual versus quarterly, and whether it rides along with the tax or sewer bill -- affects when and how the charge shows up for a household.

ours.headline: Task force previewed its full stormwater utility budget and bylaw ahead of FinCom and Select Board, taking no formal vote

watch_next: March 5 public information session on the stormwater utility bylaw
May 2026 town meeting vote on the enabling bylaw

what_happened.line: Task force will bring only a stormwater utility bylaw, not the fee, to the May 2026 town meeting.
A calendar of Finance Committee, Select Board and public sessions was set ahead of the March 16 warrant closing.
Members reviewed a draft stormwater budget with the DPW, including Chapter 90 funds and cost splits.
A member said fee revenue would largely replace an existing tax-funded stormwater line, not add a new cost outright.
One public information session is planned for March 5, with a second held in reserve for a fall town meeting.

why_it_matters: The May town meeting vote would create the legal framework for a stormwater utility; the fee and rate structure would come to a later town meeting, so this vote does not set anyone's bill.
The fee is planned to offset money the town already raises through taxes for stormwater work, so whether a resident's total bill rises depends on how much of that existing line is removed.
Residents can weigh in at the March 5 information session before the bylaw language goes to the March 16 warrant.

ours.headline: Task force plans to bring a stormwater utility bylaw (not yet the fee) to May 2026 town meeting

watch_next: Next task force meeting, January 8, 7:00 p.m.
Signing of the Weston and Samson contract and whether a kickoff meeting is scheduled

what_happened.line: The task force is finalizing its Weston and Samson consulting contract to design a townwide stormwater utility fee, after an initial cost estimate came in too high and the scope was narrowed.
No fee structure or utility design was voted on; discussion of how to tier large commercial properties and whether to credit owners who already maintain stormwater controls ended without resolution.

A resident on Zoom asked whether the consultant contract was competitively bid or awarded sole-source, and urged the task force to hold dedicated public education sessions before any fee goes back to town meeting.
The task force approved October's minutes, skipped a December meeting for the holidays, and set the next meeting for January 8.

why_it_matters: A stormwater utility fee, if the task force eventually proposes one, would be a new charge separate from the property tax levy that residents and businesses would vote on at town meeting.
How the fee tiers large commercial and impervious properties, and whether owners who already maintain their own stormwater controls get credited, will shape who pays more or less.
The contract's public-engagement scope, not yet finalized, will determine how much explanation residents get before being asked to vote on any fee.

ours.headline: Task force pushes ahead on a stormwater utility fee and the Weston & Samson study contract, with no fee structure voted yet

watch_next: November town meeting warrant article on reappropriating capital funds for the study
Task force meeting planned for the first week of December

what_happened.line: Task force voted to approve a scaled-back proposal from Weston and Sampson for a stormwater utility feasibility study.
Funding is proposed to come from reappropriating unspent money from an older capital project, via a November town meeting warrant article.
A member said the task force's current budget does not cover the revised proposal cost, though the town manager said it is covered.
Earthwork on the task force's demonstration stormwater project is complete; a kiosk and drainage grates remain to be installed.

why_it_matters: This feeds a November town meeting warrant article asking voters to reappropriate old, unspent capital funds rather than raise new money.
The study is a step toward a possible future stormwater utility fee, which could become a new charge on property owners if the town creates one.

ours.headline: Task force voted to approve a scaled-back, roughly half-cost stormwater utility study proposal from Weston and Sampson.

watch_next: Next Stormwater Task Force meeting, October 16
Reduced scope-of-work cost figure going to the Town Manager

what_happened.line: The task force cut tasks from Weston & Sampson's stormwater fee-study scope to bring a lower cost figure to the Town Manager.
Members voted to remove two tasks entirely and reduce public and progress meetings under Task 6.
Task 3 was narrowed to exclude residential and condo parcels from individual impervious-area review.
The task force will explore funding the study with a Chapter 90 highway-funds transfer instead of asking a special town meeting for money.
Prior meeting minutes were approved by roll call; the next meeting is set for October 16.

why_it_matters: This study is the first step toward a possible stormwater utility fee, a new charge that could appear on residents' bills.
Paying for the study through a Chapter 90 transfer, rather than a special town meeting, would keep that funding decision off a resident vote.
How Task 3 counts parcels -- residential included or excluded -- shapes who eventually gets assessed and billed under any future fee.

ours.headline: Task force to slash Weston & Sampson stormwater fee-study scope to fit budget, then bring it to the Town Manager

watch_next: Next Stormwater Task Force meeting, tentatively September 25th
Updated parcel spreadsheet and revised ERU tier memo from the consultant

what_happened.line: The task force found the state's impervious-area GIS data behind its proposed stormwater fee has not been updated since 2016, undercounting developed properties.
Members agreed to ask the assessor's office for parcels built or occupied since 2016 before any fee is set.
The consultant proposed adding higher ERU fee tiers after a roughly 19-acre property was found to have far more impervious area than earlier data showed.
The group weighed funding the stormwater program through a dedicated utility fee versus the DPW's operating budget, citing exposure to state MS4 fines if funding lapses.
The next meeting was moved to September 25th instead of the usual third Thursday.

why_it_matters: A new stormwater utility fee, billed by impervious surface area, is still under design and has not been set; any property owner could eventually see a line item tied to how much pavement or roof area they have.
The fee structure depends on parcel data the task force says is out of date, so which properties and how much they would owe is not yet settled.
How the stormwater program is funded -- a dedicated fee versus the town's existing operating budget -- will affect whether it appears as a new charge or as part of general tax-funded services.

ours.headline: Task force stalled on a stormwater utility fee because the underlying impervious-area data is a decade out of date

watch_next: Task force meetings August 7 and August 21 to prepare the revised property data and rate structure
Joint Select Board / Finance Committee presentation in September

what_happened.line: The consultant's property-data spreadsheet used to set stormwater fee tiers was found missing several large parcels, so no rate structure was finalized.
The task force decided to bring the fee proposal to spring annual town meeting rather than fall.
For now the four existing ERU fee tiers stay as they are rather than being expanded.
A joint posted meeting with the Select Board and Finance Committee is planned for September to present the proposal.
Stormwater fees will be billed through the town's existing utility billing system rather than a new one.

why_it_matters: This is the early shaping of a new stormwater utility fee that would appear on property tax or utility bills, separate from the tax levy and not subject to Proposition 2½.
Errors and gaps in the underlying property data mean which properties -- including large commercial parcels -- land in which fee tier is still unsettled.
Pushing the proposal to spring annual town meeting means residents will not vote on this fee until then, giving more time for the data and rate structure to be corrected first.

ours.headline: Stormwater fee rollout stalls: consultant's property data has errors and missing large parcels

watch_next: Next task force meeting, July 17, 2025
Draft utility presentation to the Select Board and Finance Committee, targeted for September/early October 2025

what_happened.line: The consultant confirmed a drafting error had made two draft fee tables disagree on tier pricing, and said one table holds the correct numbers.
The task force decided against creating an exemption or waiver process for properties claiming no stormwater runoff, citing administrative overhead.

The task force set a timeline: present the draft utility to the Select Board and Finance Committee around September, then update November town meeting, ahead of a vote planned for the 2026 annual town meeting.

Members asked the consultant for lists of the parcels in the largest fee tiers and the unclassified parcels, plus a comparison of town-owned versus private impervious area, to support the case for the fee.
The next task force meeting was set for July 17, with additional summer meetings possible to stay on the September/November schedule.

why_it_matters: This is early work on a proposed stormwater utility fee that would eventually appear as a charge to property owners, sized by how much impervious surface -- driveways, parking lots, roofs -- a parcel has.

Residents will be asked to vote on adopting the utility, with the task force aiming for the 2026 annual town meeting, so how tiers, exemptions and large-property caps are set now shapes what different property owners would eventually pay.
The tier-pricing table correction and the decision not to offer runoff exemptions are still draft choices, not a finalized fee -- both remain open to public review before any vote.

ours.headline: Task force caught a tier-pricing error in its draft stormwater fee tables and set a fall rollout timeline

watch_next: Consultant's written answers to the task force's compiled list of open questions
Next meeting, tentatively the week of June 10-12 (or July if the consultant is unavailable)

what_happened.line: The task force reviewed the consultant's proposed storm water fee tiers and rates but made no final decision, citing apparent errors in the tier pricing table.
Members leaned toward a new top tier for the largest properties and toward one fee alternative as preferred, but called both informal pending the consultant's answers.
Open questions remain on how vacant, multi-family and duplex properties would be classified and priced under the fee.
The group agreed to send the consultant a written list of outstanding questions and to compare Lunenburg's proposed tiers against Chelmsford's structure.
The next meeting is tentatively targeted for the week of June 10-12, with the consultant invited, or pushed to July if unavailable.

why_it_matters: Residents already paying the new storm water utility fee could see their tier or rate change depending on which fee alternative and tier structure the task force ultimately recommends.
Owners of vacant, multi-family, duplex or large commercial/industrial parcels have an unresolved classification question that affects what they would be billed.
No fee structure has been adopted yet, so any final proposal will still need to come back to the task force and likely to town meeting.

ours.headline: Task force debated storm water fee tiers/rates but made no final decision, awaiting consultant's answers

watch_next: The finished Annual Town Meeting presentation, due to Jen the next day
The warrant article on the stormwater utility fee at Annual Town Meeting

what_happened.line: The task force decided against naming a specific dollar figure for a proposed homeowner stormwater utility fee, opting for a "less than" framing instead.
It also chose to present that fee as a projected quarterly amount rather than an annual one, judging it more palatable to residents.
Members want the fee billed through the existing property tax bill rather than a separate mailing, pending confirmation with the town treasurer.
Soil test pits may force a redesign of the library stormwater project, the group was told.
The group approved its prior meeting's minutes and voted to adjourn.

why_it_matters: If adopted, a stormwater utility fee would be a new charge added to residents' and businesses' property tax bills, tiered by lot or impervious surface area.
This fee has not been set or voted on; it is being shaped for a warrant article at the upcoming Annual Town Meeting, where residents will get a vote.
How the fee is billed and administered still depends on confirmation from the town treasurer, so the mechanics remain unsettled.

ours.headline: Task force drafted its Town Meeting pitch for a stormwater utility fee, floating figures under $100/year but not committing.

page.overview:
Welcome to the Lunenburg Stormwater Task Force. The Stormwater Task Force is charged with the development of a comprehensive stormwater management plan that complies with state and federal regulations, provides a storm and surface water system that controls damage from storms, protects surface water quality and the environment. The plan shall determine which local agency or agencies will be responsible for implementation, establish the estimated cost of the program, as well as provide for the creation of an ongoing funding source to enable its success.
The Stormwater Task Force held its initial meeting on January 27, 2016.
We will provide information for citizens as we search through the plethora of data out there to determine what will be most useful. Please do not hesitate to email suggestions for inclusion.
All members are appointed by the Select Board. The group includes one member from the Select Board, Conservation Commission, and Planning Board. The Select Board voted to add two citizens-at-large (who live on local lakes) to the Stormwater Task Force in November 2021.
Learn more about the Stormwater Task Force (PDF)
Overview of Stormwater and the Stormwater Task Force- YouTube
The Town of Lunenburg is seeking information from residents and businesses regarding their knowledge of stormwater-related issues in the community. In order to better understand what the Town must do to inform residents and businesses, we ask that you complete the following questionnaire and return it either electronically or in hard copy.
2019 Stormwater Survey
